Gay candidates won where it was supposed to be impossible

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.
  • In a recent development, the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table.
  • And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

In a recent development, the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

Sources indicate that in 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

According to recent reports, put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

Industry observers note that this is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

Industry observers note that but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

We need your help to stay independent.

In a recent development, the refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of Newly introduced Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just mentioned for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a latest one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

Europe Steps Into the Breach on Ukraine

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Understanding the conflict four years in.

In a recent development, now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

The Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

Sources indicate that now that the Trump administration appears to have turned unequivocally against Kyiv and in favor of Moscow, it falls to Europe to backstop Ukraine’s survival. This week will be crucial, with the European Council meeting on Nov. 26-27 to decide on an additional loan of 45 billion euros (about $49.5 billion) to tide Ukraine over next year as it wrestles with nonstop missile strikes, jet-powered drones, and a gaping hole in its budget.

In a recent development, the Trump administration has, since the start of its second term, been implacably hostile to Kyiv, from Oval Office beatdowns to a relaxation of sanctions on Russia to demands that Ukraine desist from carrying out long-range strikes against Russian oil facilities. That hostility, like the war, has only escalated, with U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports (in a bid to lower fuel prices) and neutering the latest legislation meant to economically punish Moscow.

“It began with the diesel deal. This is the longest sustained effort by Team Trump” to put its thumb on the scales, mentioned John Herbst, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “It annoys me even more that they are helping [Russian President Vladimir] Putin do this. Putin wants to undermine NATO, and that is why it is so frustrating.”.

It has been revealed that trump had previously adumbrated his approach to Ukraine by delaying approval of the bipartisan legislation, championed by former Sen. Lindsey Graham, that would have levied stiff tariffs on Russia’s trading partners and put additional sanctions on top Russian officials. When the legislation finally did pass, Trump watered it down, waiving the sanctions and for once forgetting about tariffs.

“I found U.S. policy over the last six weeks depressing,” said Steven Pifer, another former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “I think Trump is lost to the cause, even if the American people are not.”.

It has been revealed that now it falls to Europe to fill the gap, both in terms of Kyiv’s budget and its defense needs. About half of the latest loan is earmarked for Ukraine’s administration and the other half for defense procurement.

Sources indicate that the European loan is not a done deal. There are four holdouts among the usual suspects—Hungary, Slovakia, Bulgaria, and the Czech Republic—that are leery of signing onto more blocwide debt to support a country they view askance. But by Friday, informed observers say, the European Union will probably be able to hammer through a fresh 45 billion on top of the 90 billion euro loan for Ukraine that it is still doling out.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has noted the latest loan would be backed by frozen Russian assets held in Europe. Those central bank assets total about $300 billion worldwide, with just over $200 billion in Belgium. Despite years of posturing, four years into the war, neither Europe nor the United States nor the United Kingdom has moved from freezing to seizing, fearful of the potential legal, financial, and other consequences of grabbing illicit Russian money. That makes the ultimate collateral for this fresh European loan something of a question mark.

It has been revealed that “Europe has no choice but to fund Ukraine’s defense. The question is how you do it,” stated Timothy Ash, a Russia expert at Chatham House. “I find it incredible, when you put it across like this, which taxpayers should pay for this: Europe’s or Russia’s?” (He has some thoughts.).

Industry observers note that the bigger question is broader. Europe knows that enabling Ukraine to survive the war, or at least avoid a dishonorable peace, is critical to the country’s survival as well as its own. The problem, which has been apparent since January 2025, is that Ukraine and Europe are on their own. The United States has not provided any fresh financial support for Kyiv since Trump came back to office, has at times interrupted intelligence-sharing and satellite links, and continues to block the sale of much-need missile interceptors held in European inventories.

In a recent development, U.S. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby scolded Ukraine last week for striking Russian oil facilities, arguing that such attacks were ineffective. (Ukraine’s long-range strikes have taken offline about half of Russia’s refinery capacity in recent months, cratered its energy exports, and are leading to lines at gas stations in Russia.) Meanwhile, Russian missiles and drones continue to rain down on Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other major cities.

“Trump is just defending Putin and making it harder for Ukraine to defend itself,” Herbst said.

Germany’s vocal support for mobilizing hundreds of billions of Moscow’s reserves could be a game-changer for Ukraine.

For all the talk of a newly introduced world order, the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting produced little of substance.

According to recent reports, one question that looms now is whether Europe’s determination to support Ukraine—Europe has already provided nearly 240 billion euros (about $260 billion), far more than the United States or any other country—will push Trump into reprisal mode. He has in the past slapped tariffs on Europe while waiving penalties on Russia. Over the weekend, Trump posted a photo of himself with Putin titled, simply, “My Friend.”.

Industry observers note that “If Trump wants to go down that route, it might get ugly in Europe, but I don’t think Europe can afford to let Ukraine lose. There is a real understanding in Europe about how high the stakes are for them,” Ash said.

Recent findings suggest that “It will be interesting to see where this goes in terms of the U.S.-EU relationship. This could be a huge crisis. We have to see how far he is willing to take this.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Sources indicate that itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

It has been revealed that when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Sources indicate that over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

Industry observers note that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

According to recent reports, the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

Recent findings suggest that A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. A brief summit between the leaders of China, the United States, and Russia was held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Critics saw little substantive achievement, arguing that the three had merely taken advantage of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum to meet for a photo opportunity. Some American observers faulted U.S. President Donald Trump in particular for yielding to China and Russia rather than showing leadership.

In my view, the summit, short as it was, did matter. In great-power politics, the format can sometimes matter more than the concrete results. The leaders of the three countries had never sat down together in this format; that they managed to do so says something about the kind of era that we are entering.

It has been revealed that in an era of great-power politics, one of the keys to avoiding military conflict is for the powers to hear one another out. They did so in Shenzhen. They also exceeded expectations by issuing a joint peace declaration with four points of agreement. And for Chinese President Xi Jinping in particular, the summit offered a first chance to try out an approach to great-power relations that he had originally proposed to Washington, this time with both the United States and Russia at the table.

Yet while Xi hosted, the biggest winner was clearly Russian President Vladimir Putin. The war in Ukraine has left Russia diplomatically isolated from much of the West. Shenzhen could not end that isolation, but it indicated that Russia could not simply be shut out of great-power diplomacy. Russia is a major military power and rich in natural resources, but its overall strength still falls well short of that of the United States or China. By sitting down with Putin as an equal, the Chinese and American leaders acknowledged that Russia remains a power that they cannot bypass on questions of global strategic security.

Xi was a winner, too. Beijing indicated that it could bring two adversaries, the United States and Russia, together on Chinese soil and secure a joint declaration. The format itself put China back at the center of the international stage. A decade ago, it would have been hard to imagine China convening such a meeting. That also helped Xi’s standing at home.

Trump had just suffered a crushing defeat in the midterm elections. Yet both China and Russia accorded him the respect due an American president with whom they could still discuss strategic matters. China, in particular, gave him a lavish welcome rather than treating him as a lame duck.

But the three leaders did not sit around a table simply for the sake of appearances, and Xi in particular made some meaningful gains here. The Chinese president raised the question of how the three powers should deal with one another from here on. His answer: with mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, mutually beneficial cooperation, and dialogue and consultation.

These are principles that Beijing has long pressed in its dealings with Washington, rooted in Xi’s proposal for a “new type of great-power relations” between China and the United States. As host, Xi set the tone by extending that framework to all three countries. The summit was a chance for Beijing to put it into practice. In effect, Xi brought Putin into the room to press Trump on an approach that he had long advocated for U.S.-China relations.

That, from Beijing’s perspective, was the summit’s most important achievement. Rivalry between Washington and Beijing, and outright hostility between Washington and Moscow, did not prevent the three countries from coordinating on strategic stability.

This takes a minimum of trust. None of the three countries has to believe that its rivals will give up competing. Each has to believe that the others also want to prevent a miscalculation from triggering a conflict, that they are willing to explain their intentions, and that they will listen when another country spells out its red lines. Sitting down together, rather than meeting only in pairs, means letting down their guard enough to acknowledge that some risks involve all three and cannot necessarily be managed through bilateral talks alone.

If regular coordination takes hold, then Shenzhen will matter even more to Beijing. After the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi remarked that China would stay in touch with Russia and the United States at the working level. That is a start. Whether the leaders’ dialogue lasts will depend on whether they meet a second or third time, and whether communication holds up when relations come under strain.

Those gains stem largely from the format. The declaration itself offers further clues to what Beijing wanted to accomplish. The first, third, and fourth points are particularly revealing.

The first concerns U.N. reform. The three countries agreed to work toward reforming the United Nations so it could respond more effectively to global challenges and better fulfill its basic mission of maintaining international peace and security.

Industry observers note that my reading is that Beijing pushed for this language to reassure the global south. Beijing knows that some countries in the global south are uneasy about China sitting down with the United States and Russia at a summit of its own making. Putting the U.N. reform first sent a related message: The three powers had met to help the United Nations fulfill its peace and security mandate and had no intention of making upcoming rules over the heads of the global south. Wang’s insistence after the summit that countries large and small are equal was meant to convey the same point.

In a recent development, the third point in the declaration names the International Criminal Court. The leaders emphasized the importance of state consent and respect for the immunity of state officials, and they noted the court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction. Moscow likely pushed for this provision in response to the court’s arrest warrant for Putin, backed by Trump due to the U.S. far right’s hostility toward the court. But the words “and other similar bodies” were most likely added at Beijing’s insistence. They give China a joint statement that it can cite in future disputes over jurisdiction, such as the South China Sea arbitration.

Industry observers note that those words also have implications for Taiwan. If mainland China were to attack Taiwan and Washington were to push for Chinese leaders to be held criminally accountable for alleged war crimes, Beijing could point to a declaration the United States helped concern and ask: What did you say in Shenzhen about state consent and the immunity of officials?

It has been revealed that the fourth point can be read as a gain for Beijing on nuclear issues. The three countries reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought—language that originated with U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, but that has been taken up by China. They also agreed to hold talks on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

Sources indicate that trump wanted trilateral nuclear disarmament talks. What made it into the declaration was language on risk reduction and nonproliferation. Beijing succeeded in redirecting U.S. pressure to join disarmament talks toward concerns that all three countries might be willing to keep discussing.

According to recent reports, china also gained a basis for putting diplomatic pressure on Japan, where changes to—or even the abandonment of—the three non-nuclear principles are under consideration. If Tokyo goes down that path, particularly if the debate turns to Japan acquiring nuclear weapons of its own, Beijing can cite the trilateral agreement and press Washington to say where it stands on those risks.

Industry observers note that xi revealed at Shenzhen that China could convene two adversaries, set a framework for discussing strategic stability, and get them to agree on some common positions. As much criticism as the meeting drew, it also raised hopes that trilateral talks might become a regular fixture. Xi’s remarks suggest that he would like to see that happen. The real test will come when the three countries face a crisis and their interests collide. Will they still be willing to talk the way that they did in Shenzhen?

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

  • Christian Schneider is a National Review contributor and writes the Anti-Knowledge newsletter.

In a recent development, to relieve stress nowadays, modern high school students may fire up a game of Grand Theft Auto VI or bring a puppy dog to class. But in the recent past, American high schools would set aside a patch of blacktop where tense teenagers could fire up a couple of heaters between classes, presumably so nobody would show up to fourth-period algebra in nicotine withdrawal. Understanding that there was nothing they could do to prevent kids from lighting up, schools in the 1970s and 1980s frequently had smoking courts. The calculation was that they might as well keep the students in their line of sight.

In those days, airplane passengers could light up while in flight, swathing 150 strangers inside a metal tube at 30,000 feet in Pall Mall smoke from Milwaukee to Phoenix.

Tech Giants Are Effectively Ungovernable. Here’s How to Change That.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

  • Recent findings suggest that american business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In a recent development, american business has minted a upcoming brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Recent findings suggest that american business has minted a new brand of executive: the CEO who is too big to fire. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s board declared that it had accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang, felled by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and a romance with one of the executive’s own subordinates. Six days later, Huang was back, restored after a unanimous vote by the same board. Nvidia’s shares soared. Many investors celebrated the return of the leather-jacketed founder credited with making the manufacturer the engine of the artificial intelligence revolution.

It has been revealed that three years earlier, OpenAI’s board had dismissed Sam Altman, citing a lack of candor with directors. Five days later, Altman returned, and most of the directors responsible for his removal were out.

According to recent reports, in both cases, directors discovered that formal authority to remove a chief executive does not mean the power to do so in practice. The episodes exposed a three-pronged weakness in corporate governance: the challenge of maverick founders, the extraordinary complexity of AI, and the growing dependence of the U.S. economy and national security on a handful of companies at the technological frontier.

Recent findings suggest that both Altman and Huang have personas, know-how, and market-moving power that made them unfireable. Yet if the boards of the country’s most consequential technology firms cannot exercise ultimate authority over management, these companies are effectively ungovernable. This reveals a major gap in corporate stewardship, underscoring the imperative of robust regulation to ensure that the vulnerabilities of powerful U.S. companies do not become fatal weaknesses for the country’s democracy and society writ large.

Industry observers note that the iconic corporate founder is a hallmark of U.S. business culture. Henry Ford and Andrew Carnegie shaped society-altering industries around their personalities and distinctive working styles. Steve Jobs provides the most celebrated historic example of this type of figure in tech. Forced out of Apple in 1985, Jobs returned in 1997 when the organization was in steep decline. His track record of inventiveness helped win back employees, customers, investors, and developers. He also persuaded Bill Gates to invest $150 million in Apple and commit to developing Microsoft software for Macintosh computers, building an ecosystem whose fortunes were intertwined with his own and that has dominated the market for decades.

Sources indicate that these bold founders may have as much in common with an artist or creator than they do with fellow CEOs. A great architect or film director works with large teams but puts an unmistakable stamp on their work. Although a studio or tradition can continue after its originator dies or departs, investors, collaborators, and audiences do not always stay on.

This analogy helps explain why succession at frontier technology companies is so fraught. Investors bet on a founder’s judgment about technologies whose commercial potential is unproven. Engineers are inspired by a particular visionary. Customers and business partners invest in the future that the founder promises. As these forces rally, they reify perceptions of an individual’s genius, which attracts still more talent and capital. Confidence becomes self-perpetuating.

Sources indicate that such devotion is measurable. Huang topped Glassdoor’s 2026 ranking of CEOs with a 99 percent approval rating among employee reviewers. Thousands of employees reportedly signed a letter seeking his reinstatement this month. His reportedly cruel behavior toward certain employees seemingly did little to puncture that aura.

OpenAI’s 2023 crisis demonstrated the power of such fealty. After its board fired Altman, more than 95 percent of the company’s employees signed a letter threatening to resign unless he came back. Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest commercial partner, rolled out a red carpet to Altman, promising to allow him to rebuild his team there. Faced with losing the workforce that was OpenAI’s principal asset, the board folded. The employees, investors, and commercial partners whose confidence had helped make Altman successful overpowered those charged with supervising him.

In a recent development, these examples do not prove that founders are irreplaceable. Apple’s revenues more than doubled during the early years of John Sculley’s post-Jobs tenure in the 1980s; more recently, the firm has thrived under Tim Cook since Jobs’s death. When Uber’s Travis Kalanick was forced out in 2017, investors worried about losing the transportation innovator’s aggressive founder. His successor, Dara Khosrowshahi, now presides over a company that generated $193 billion in gross bookings and $10 billion in free cash flow in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that board members are a little like grandparents. They admire and care about the baby, comforted that the parent—the CEO—does the daily grind. When the parent disappears, the board is left holding a crying, demanding infant. Sedate quarterly meetings suddenly turn into frantic round-the-clock Zooms. Having lost the one person who they trusted to raise the child, boards want nothing more than to once again pass the progeny into capable hands.

When it comes to AI companies, the problem is magnified by the extraordinary gap between a CEO’s knowledge of frontier technologies and what even accomplished directors can understand. Nvidia’s 10-person board includes Melissa Lora, the former president of Taco Bell; Stephen Neal, a distinguished trial lawyer; and Dawn Hudson, a former Pepsi-Cola and National Football League marketing executive. Three of the 10 have served on the board for more than 28 years each. Just one is under the age of 60. While several board members have technology backgrounds, the emergence of Nvidia’s chips and financing as lynchpins of AI competition has transformed the demands on a group of directors who were chosen at least in part because Huang trusted them not to get in his way. Alongside bleeding-edge technologies, the board is now dealing with matters of foreign espionage, regulatory capture, securities fraud, and export controls. It’s not hard to imagine Nvidia’s directors feeling out of their depth.

The governance challenges created by Nvidia’s technological complexity are compounded by the manufacturer’s centrality to the U.S. economy and national security. A 2026 investment analysis estimated that 42 AI-related stocks accounted for 60 percent of the S&P 500’s gains in 2025. By September 2026, Nvidia alone represented approximately 8.4 percent of the index. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday propelled a broader market rally, underscoring how closely U.S. financial fortunes have become tied to confidence in the AI industry. The national-security dependence is at least as consequential. AI is increasingly incorporated into military intelligence, surveillance, cyber operations, logistics, and command-and-control systems. Access to advanced computing is at the heart of competitive tensions with China.

Industry observers note that these dependencies help explain U.S. President Donald Trump’s extraordinary intervention in Nvidia’s leadership deliberations. According to Semafor, the president called into a Nvidia board meeting to press for Huang’s return, suggesting that China might recruit him if Nvidia failed to take him back. Though no investigation has been completed and the allegations of Chinese plotting to compromise Huang are alarming, Trump personally vouched that his return would pose no national security risk. It is hard to know who possesses greater leverage in the Trump-Huang relationship—the president who controls regulatory decisions or the corporate titan whose technology is essential to domestic prosperity and national security.

In a recent development, reliance on individual technology entrepreneurs for vital national functions can compromise public interests. In October, Ukrainian forces experienced serious disruptions to Starshield satellite communications, impairing military operations. Elon Musk subsequently acknowledged that his company, SpaceX, had restricted certain uses of the service, though responsibility for the disruptions remains contested. Society depends on interconnected technological systems that are vulnerable to malfunction and compromise; the power vested in a handful of tech moguls who control these networks is staggering.

Industry observers note that U.S. institutions have failed to reckon with this amalgamation of power. Congress remains divided over how to regulate AI. Federal agencies possess fragmented authority over specific risks and no mandate from the White House to address them. Companies develop capabilities faster than public institutions can assess them. CEOs with immense technical resources and public influence end up guiding the officials responsible for overseeing them.

Industry observers note that the consequences of this glaring void will reverberate internationally. U.S. corporate leadership is predicated on the perception that U.S. companies operate within a system of enforceable laws, strong oversight, and credible government institutions. This distinguishes U.S. technology from Chinese alternatives, whose governance remains vulnerable to direct state intervention. But if U.S. boards cannot meaningfully restrain powerful executives, and the president can intervene in their internal deliberations, those differentiators collapse. Governments considering whose AI infrastructure to trust will ask whether U.S. companies offer genuine institutional safeguards.

The obvious response is to strengthen corporate oversight. Some mechanisms already exist. Nvidia has an independent board, audit and governance committees, and a confidential reporting hotline. It has now added a specialized national security committee and is upgrading its compliance function. OpenAI maintains a safety and security committee overseeing its operations. But all these arrangements depend on directors whose authority may be subsumed by founder loyalty, commercial pressure, and technological complexity.

Other highly regulated industries offer more robust, proven oversight models. Under Federal Reserve rules, large bank holding companies must maintain independent risk committees, including directors with relevant expertise; chief risk officers report directly to those committees as well as management. Britain requires senior executives at financial firms to be approved by regulators, makes it clear what each is responsible for, and can hold them personally accountable if they fail to take reasonable steps to prevent wrongdoing. U.S. pharmaceutical regulation provides another precedent. Federal rules give drug manufacturers’ quality-control arms the authority to approve or reject products and manufacturing procedures, so that decisions do not lie simply with a CEO’s commercial preferences.

These models suggest an approach to governing companies whose technologies pose exceptional public risks. Congress should establish an independent federal supervisory authority for designated frontier AI companies, including critical infrastructure providers and developers of exceptionally capable models. Its jurisdiction should depend on the risks and systemic importance of technology companies, rather than their size or public-firm status. Now that corporate interests have captured the U.S. executive branch, legislative oversight is essential.

Sources indicate that such an institution would need permanent technical staff with expertise in advanced computing, model capabilities, cybersecurity, and intelligence threats. It would require secure access to proprietary information, the power to inspect governance systems, and the authority to compel corrective action. Its independence from day-to-day political intervention would be essential.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, regulated companies should have dedicated board-level risk committees staffed by directors with technical and national-security competence. Those committees should retain their own expert advisors and receive regular reports from both the CEO and independent risk, safety, and compliance officers. Boards should be required to document how they evaluate consequential decisions, oversee potential conflicts of interest, and prepare for abrupt leadership transitions.

A further priority is genuine protection for whistleblowers. Nvidia’s formal policies prohibit retaliation, yet recent reporting suggests that employees fear speaking openly. In technology companies, confidentiality is increasingly difficult to preserve. Employers can potentially reconstruct a source’s identity from records of device use, badge access, communications, and document activity, even when a reporter or investigator promises anonymity. One shudders to think what this might mean for Nvidia employees who recently spoke out about mistreatment or alleged misdeeds, believing that Huang’s tenure was over for good.

In a recent development, A modern whistleblower regime should offer secure channels outside the company, enforceable restrictions on attempts to identify confidential sources, and meaningful penalties for retaliation. An independent regulator should interview employees and business partners without requiring them to expose themselves to management. Such protections are particularly important during investigations involving a powerful founder.

It may be tempting to conclude that Nvidia’s crisis ended happily once Huang returned and the market rallied. The OpenAI episode invited a similar reaction, especially as the manufacturer continued its rapid expansion after Altman’s reinstatement. But neither recovery resolves the institutional weakness that allowed directors’ decisions to be reversed under pressure.

Sources indicate that U.S. technological leadership cannot depend on a system in which the most influential executives are effectively irreplaceable. A manufacturer that is too massive to lose its founder may also be too powerful to govern itself. As AI becomes embedded in the economy, national security, and public life, the United States needs oversight institutions capable of withstanding the demands of employees, investors, politicians, and even the most celebrated innovators. The long-term credibility of U.S. technological leadership will depend on it.

She is the author of Dare to Speak: Defending Free Speech for All. X: @SuzanneNossel.

  • Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.
  • The concern also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh prepares to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., is among Democrats looking to take a harder line on AI and chip exports in the fresh year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Incoming Democratic leaders called for tighter semiconductor export controls and investigations of the Trump administration Monday as Nvidia reinstated disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

The concern also spilled into the party’s Senate majority leader election fight, as Democrats weigh prepares to advance bills in the 120th Congress that would regulate artificial intelligence.

The reinstatement of Huang came as President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday the CEO “did nothing wrong” and that he had been “speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly.”.

Industry observers note that in a Monday statement, Nvidia remarked its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who is challenging Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., for the majority leader role, told reporters Monday that in the “first 100 days” of the newly introduced Congress, he wants Senate rules changed to allow for faster floor consideration of bills that had broad bipartisan support in committee.

He also supports legislation to require independent mandatory evaluations of AI systems and updates to liability laws to account not just for harm caused by AI models but for risks of internal development. He also mentioned a bill he sponsored that he said would ensure other electricity consumers don’t bear the costs of data center construction.

Van Hollen also said that Congress should create a special joint committee on AI to consider the technology’s broader impacts, including on the workforce and economy.

“I think we need to move urgently on the safety piece and then move with deliberation, but also speed, on tackling these other issues,” Van Hollen said.

In a recent development, last week, Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., wrote to Van Hollen and Schumer proposing a joint committee to “complement” the work of committees of jurisdiction and asking for their plans for AI if they were elected leader.

Speaking to reporters and in his reply to Hickenlooper, Van Hollen also supported greater transparency into the AI industry’s financing and debt structure and tighter export controls on advanced chips like those sold by Nvidia. In particular, he said the Commerce Department should close “loopholes” for remote access to chips and purchase by affiliates of companies banned from directly acquiring sensitive technologies.

Schumer, in a post on X Monday, noted Democrats would “work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer wrote.

In a recent development, house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., whose caucus officially backed him last week to be speaker in the new year, seconded the need for investigations into Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. He also supported export controls.

“The National Defense Authorization Act must include ironclad export control legislation to prevent powerful AI technology from being exploited by the Chinese Communist Party and other adversaries,” Jeffries wrote, referring to the pending fiscal 2027 defense policy bill.

In a recent development, A manager’s amendment to the Senate’s version of the bill includes several chip export restrictions, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House-passed NDAA does not contain similar language.

Meanwhile, Republican committee leaders pressed forward with looks to bring in Huang for questioning.

Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Monday confirmed plans for a Dec. 3 hearing titled “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls” featuring Huang as a witness.

Recent findings suggest that "Mr. Huang’s testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be critical for protecting America’s AI advantage,” Scott stated in a statement. “The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing.".

According to recent reports, scott previously invited Lutnick to testify before the committee on Dec. 10.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who looks likely to hold the banking gavel next Congress, said Huang’s return as CEO “only increases the urgency” of export controls.

In a recent development, “The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the tech giant’s board still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” Warren mentioned in a statement.

House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said in a social media video on Monday that Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter would sit for transcribed interviews with his committee and with the House Intelligence Committee and Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party the week of Nov. 30.

The committees also requested that Commerce Undersecretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the panels.

John T. Bennett contributed to this report.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Recent findings suggest that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at delayed U.S. Patriot air defense missile shipments to Ukraine, Israeli forces killing a top Hamas official, and yet another purge within China’s leadership.

As Russia batters Ukraine’s cities with missile strikes, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has delayed sending scores of Patriot air defense missiles to the embattled country, including those held by European nations, according to a Financial Times report.

Industry observers note that welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at delayed U.S. Patriot air defense missile shipments to Ukraine, Israeli forces killing a top Hamas official, and yet another purge within China’s leadership.

As Russia batters Ukraine’s cities with missile strikes, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has delayed sending scores of Patriot air defense missiles to the embattled country, including those held by European nations, according to a Financial Times report.

According to recent reports, in total, the U.S. has held up around 60 Patriot air defense missiles, including more advanced PAC-3 missiles as well as around 20 PAC-2 missiles. The missiles include those that are already held in European stockpiles but require U.S. sign-off before their transfer.

Industry observers note that the missile transfers were originally set to occur in September, October, and November in batches of around 10 missiles each. A further delivery is set for December. Ukraine began sounding the alarm publicly in October.

Patriot air defense missiles are Ukraine’s primary defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Russia has used in an accelerating campaign to make Ukraine’s major cities unlivable.

Since September, Russia has attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure more than 350 times, frequently resulting in days with no regular supply of power or water, a growing concern as winter approaches. The Pentagon is separately delaying approving a plan to allow Ukraine to produce its own Patriot missiles domestically.

Recent findings suggest that the slowed deliveries follow interruptions in recent weeks to the functioning of Starshield, a version of the Starlink satellite internet service that Ukraine relies on for battlefield communication. Ukraine uses Starshield in its mid-range strike drones, as well as in systems used to defend against jet-powered Russian attack drones. Starshield is owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Musk and the Trump administration have traded blame over who is responsible for the throttling of Ukraine’s Starshield access.

Even as Russia scores wins in its missile campaign against Ukraine, however, recently leaked data and Ukraine’s own strikes illustrate the high price Moscow is paying.

Sources indicate that russia has lost at least 490,000 soldiers, according to data derived from a leaked Russian government database and analyzed by independent Russian news outlet Meduza. Even that may be an underestimate—a further 230,000 are listed as missing in action, many of whom are likely dead but not yet officially recorded as such. That means that as many as 720,000 may have died in Ukraine. The losses place the war in Ukraine as the deadliest conflict for Russia since World War II.

Russia primarily sends volunteers to fight in Ukraine and pays large bonuses as an incentive. While Russia has so far been able to find enough volunteers to staff its army, the losses are an economic and social strain on the country. Data compiled by Janis Kluge, an expert on Russian recruitment, reveals a slowdown in recruiting for October as compared to last year.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s long-range strike capacity continues to develop. On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine was behind a strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. Ukrainian drone also recently attacked a Russian warship docked at a port in Libya. Ukraine on Tuesday separately launched yet another mass wave of strikes on Russia, with Russia stating that it shot down 699 drones.

Deadly airstrikes. Israeli forces have “eliminated” Naim Abu Nahal, the head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz announced in a joint statement posted on X on Tuesday. Nahal took on the role in September, after Israeli forces seized his predecessor in a Gaza ground operation and took him to Israel. “No terrorist will succeed in evading the long arm of the State of Israel,” the statement added.

The Israeli military also rolled out two airstrikes that killed six other people in Gaza on Tuesday, including a teenage boy and two police officers, who were killed at a police station, according to Palestinian health officials and first responders. Gaza’s police force slammed what it called “an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos,” the BBC reported; Israeli forces noted they struck “military operatives.”.

Sources indicate that corruption probe. A top Chinese Communist Party official once considered a possible successor to Chinese leader Xi Jinping is being investigated “for suspected severe violations of discipline and laws,” Xinhua reported on Tuesday, in the latest example of ongoing purges of China’s leadership.

In a recent development, the official, Chen Jining, is the head of the Communist Party in Shanghai, China’s most populous city and a key economic center. He is also a member of China’s Politburo, an elite group of 24 officials that help lead the country. He had been seen as likely to rise within the ranks of China’s government, having previously served as mayor of Beijing.

The move is part of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign that has seen hundreds of top officials, including many within the military, convicted. Since 2025, three other members of the Politburo have also faced corruption charges, and in the last two months, corruption charges were confirmed against both Beijing’s deputy mayor and the former mayor of major city Chongqing.

Xi’s consolidation of power comes ahead of a likely fourth term as president beginning next year, meaning that he will hold power until at least 2032.

Money up front. Japan will pay its full contribution to the International Criminal ​Court (ICC) ahead of schedule following an appeal by the court after the United States sanctioned it, according to Prime Minister Sanae ‌Takaichi.

Japan is one of the largest contributors to the court, accounting for around 15 percent of its funding. The early payment will give the court a larger financial cushion after U.S. sanctions take effect in April 2027.

It has been revealed that the Trump administration rolled out a campaign against the ICC in July, starting with pressuring other nations to withdraw from it. That effort has been largely unsuccessful, with only four countries—Tajikistan, Chad, Venezuela, and Naoero—leaving the court. In October, the United States sanctioned the ICC itself, which U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called a “rogue court.”.

It has been revealed that the United States has long been concerned about the ICC’s ability to prosecute U.S. soldiers. However, the Trump administration’s pressure on the ICC represents the sharpest attack yet on the body.

Sunset today will see the appearance of a supermoon, during which the celestial body will be about 30 percent brighter and nearly 20 percent larger than normal. In North America, a full moon that falls after Nov. 7 is known as a “beaver” moon, as it usually occurs around when beavers are building their dams and stocking up on food. If you happen to miss this month’s supermoon, though, don’t worry: There are three more coming in a row in December, January, and February, according to NASA. Happy moongazing!

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

The photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss. There are multiple portraits of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan with U.S. President Donald Trump in the White House last year; pictures of Pashinyan and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Yerevan from February of that same year, when Vance became the senior-most sitting U.S. official to visit Armenia; and photos of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his visit to Yerevan last May. There are also multiple pictures of the Oval Office prayer meeting organized by the embassy in September, where Trump met with leaders from the Armenian Christian community in the United States.

I asked if they change the photographs with each administration, and the embassy’s spokesperson informed me that this is the first time any photographs have been put up—to mark the momentous nature of the Trump administration’s relationship with Armenia.

Recent findings suggest that the photographs lining the walls of the stairs of the Armenian Embassy in Washington are impossible to miss. There are multiple portraits of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan with U.S. President Donald Trump in the White House last year; pictures of Pashinyan and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Yerevan from February of that same year, when Vance became the senior-most sitting U.S. official to visit Armenia; and photos of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during his visit to Yerevan last May. There are also multiple pictures of the Oval Office prayer meeting organized by the embassy in September, where Trump met with leaders from the Armenian Christian community in the United States.

I asked if they change the photographs with each administration, and the embassy’s spokesperson informed me that this is the first time any photographs have been put up—to mark the momentous nature of the Trump administration’s relationship with Armenia.

It has been revealed that trump brokered the signing of a joint declaration in August 2025 between Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, which committed Armenia and Azerbaijan to resolving their decadeslong violent conflict over disputed territories. It’s one of several wars that Trump claimed to have solved during his second term as he lobbied for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the two countries have yet to sign a formal peace agreement more than a year later.

“The final peace deal is not there, but we have peace on the ground,” Armenian Ambassador Narek Mkrtchyan stated. “We have trade relations with Azerbaijan right now—we are buying some stuff from them, they are buying from us—and this is very crucial for the peace. Of course, there are still some issues that need to be addressed, but in general, peace is in the region.”.

Monday marked movement on two of the biggest outstanding complications.

Sources indicate that armenia put forward a draft proposal of its new constitution that removes language calling for reunification with the Nagorno-Karabakh region, a disputed territory within Azerbaijan that was controlled by ethnic Armenians until an Azerbaijani military offensive deposed them in 2023. Pashinyan has supported the new constitution—which Azerbaijan has demanded as a condition to reach a permanent peace deal—and has stated that he will resign if a referendum to adopt it fails.

The second development was the official launch of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a roughly 27-mile transit corridor between Azerbaijan and its exclave of Nakhchivan that was agreed (and rebranded from the “Zangezur corridor”) during the joint declaration in Washington last August. The TRIPP corridor passes through Armenian territory and will be controlled by the Armenian government, though it only retains a 26 percent stake in the corridor’s development—the remaining 74 percent will be held by the U.S. government.

Mkrtchyan, who previously served as the Pashinyan government’s minister for labor and social affairs, was appointed to be the country’s ambassador to Washington in late August 2025, just weeks after the Trump-brokered accord with Azerbaijan was signed.

“The current agenda that we have with the United States of America, we never had before,” he said.

Armenia has high hopes from Trump and TRIPP. “It actually has the potential to change the concept of the South Caucasus. Previously, this region has always been associated with conflict, with instability,” Mkrtchyan said. “This region has the potential to turn into a territory of dialogue, of connectivity, of prosperity, and cooperation, and the TRIPP project is an organic component of this.”.

Industry observers note that mkrtchyan also corrected me when I referred to TRIPP as a “corridor,” describing it instead as an “infrastructure project route” with “roads, railroads, fiber optics, transmission lines, possibly pipelines.” TRIPP is now “becoming more than a bilateral project” for peace and connectivity between Armenia and Azerbaijan, he mentioned, and will eventually turn into a key trade passage between Central Asia and Europe—entirely under Armenian jurisdiction. “It’s going to be a fresh global supply chain,” Mkrtchyan said.

Those ambitions could run headlong into Armenia’s geopolitical reality. The landlocked country also shares a 193-mile land border with Turkey that has remained closed since 1993, when Armenia’s conflict with Azerbaijan first began. “Right now, 80 percent of Armenia’s borders are closed,” Mkrtchyan noted, adding that talks to reopen the Turkish border continue in parallel with the Azerbaijan negotiations, “and there is a lot of hope and a lot of potential.”.

Then there is Armenia’s 27-mile border with Iran that the TRIPP route runs uncomfortably close to. Iran has bristled at the prospect of having a U.S.-led initiative so close to its territory while Tehran and Washington remain at war, and a senior advisor to Iran’s supreme leader warned this week that “if Trump and his allies want to cross this Iranian red line, we will break their legs.” Armenia’s entire railway system is also still controlled by Russia—a legacy of the erstwhile Soviet Union that both countries were a part of—and the once-tight relationship between Yerevan and Moscow has steadily deteriorated thanks to Russia’s war with Ukraine and a perceived lack of Russian support over Nagorno-Karabakh.

But those conflicts have only spurred Armenia to diversify from its neighbors and traditional partners by aligning more closely with Washington, according to Mkrtchyan. “This is a newly introduced reality, and we live in this new reality, but this is our strategic choice,” he mentioned. “But we were very transparent and open to our colleagues in the region—we told them that this is not against you. It’s not against Iran, it’s not against Russia. It’s first of all for Armenia’s national interests, for Armenia’s security, and for regional cooperation,” he added. “. This is a unique opportunity to transform the region.”.

Armenia is also hoping to parlay its newfound U.S. links into becoming a technology powerhouse. Earlier this year, a San Francisco manufacturer called Firebird established a fresh data center in Armenia in partnership with fellow U.S. firms Nvidia and Dell, in a deal that will be powered by 70,000 of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductor chips by the end of 2027. “We want to become a key partner of the U.S. in providing sustainable supply chains for future AI systems,” Mkrtchyan remarked. That ambition is further bolstered by nuclear cooperation and critical minerals agreements signed by Vance and Rubio during their respective visits this year.

“Especially after the peace deal, it gave a strong signal to the American companies that right now is the moment to consider Armenia as a platform for cooperation and investment,” Mkrtchyan said.

Sources indicate that given that our conversation took place just days after a resounding defeat for Trump’s Republican Party in the U.S. midterm election, officially consigning the U.S. president to lame-duck status for the remaining two years of his term, I asked Mkrtchyan how Armenia is thinking about its relationship with Washington heading into a post-Trump world.

Sources indicate that “It’s very natural that at some point, President Trump and the Trump administration will not be in power. It is also natural that in the coming 50 years, only Republicans or President Trump will not be ruling the government, because our agreement with the United States of America—the TRIPP agreement—is for 50 years,” he said, adding that historically Armenia has had “bipartisan friends” in Washington.

Sources indicate that “Of course, President Trump will always be remembered as someone who brokered this peace deal and the Armenian nation is very thankful to him,” Mkrtchyan added. “But we are building our relationships with the United States of America institutionally.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump’s lobbying for Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO is a national security scandal of unprecedented proportions, as I wrote on Monday (gift link).

Huang’s reinstatement comes less than a week after the trilateral summit among Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Trump pronounced the Chinese autocrat his personal friend and endorsed his geopolitical language.

Taken together, these events illustrate an increasingly clear reality of U.S.-China relations: Beijing knows Trump’s pressure points and isn’t afraid to exploit them. But Washington cannot do the same to Xi.

It is difficult to know how much Xi shaped Trump’s thinking on Huang. Trump was already sympathetic to Huang and receptive to the whispers of Silicon Valley leaders. But the U.S. president himself remarked he had discussed the matter with Xi; whatever the precise chain of influence, China scored a major win.

Trump’s obsequiousness toward Xi reflects China’s skillful use of both stick and carrot. Last year, Beijing’s rare-earth squeeze caused panic in Washington and forced Trump into a humiliating climbdown in the tariff war that he started. Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang was likely triggered in part by another of the president’s fears: a falling stock market.

Industry observers note that with the U.S. economy still entangled with China, Xi has the leverage to force supply-chain crises across multiple industries. He can also offer Trump praise and pageantry on the world stage to help compensate for unpopularity on the home front.

Washington, by contrast, lacks the will, knowledge, and capability to pressure Beijing. The Trump administration is bogged down in Iran, has gutted U.S. cybersecurity capabilities, and has wrecked the relationships that once gave allies the confidence to push back against China. With the Nvidia scandal, it has shown that it will abandon its own sanctions enforcement under pressure.

Industry observers note that it’s this imbalance of power that makes me skeptical of recent announcements that there will be another round of U.S. tariffs on China. As much as Trump loves tariffs, he wants Xi’s approval more.

Sources indicate that some analysts, eager to avert a so-called second Cold War, have embraced Trump’s support for reinstating Huang, on the grounds that U.S. chip policy toward China should be more permissive. This misses the point entirely. As I have argued, the real debate about U.S. chip policy needed to be held in good faith.

Trump’s decision to allow high-end chip exports to China was not the result of careful deliberation, but of straightforward corruption.

Recent findings suggest that those celebrating Huang’s return are overlooking more than the blatant violations of national-security norms, the abandonment of serious sanctions enforcement, and Trump’s personal financial interest in Nvidia. They are also ignoring the lessons of the recent past.

China hawks made a moral and strategic blunder by backing Trump during his first term when his interests seemed aligned with theirs. It would be even more foolish for China doves to do the same today.

In a recent development, politburo member purged. On Tuesday, Xi purged yet another senior official: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. As is customary, the news broke with an announcement that Chen was under investigation for severe violations of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) discipline. His fall brings the number of Politburo members eliminated since last year to four, out of an original 24 members in 2022.

Unlike most of his contemporaries, Chen is a genuine intellectual. An environmental engineer with a Ph.D. from Imperial College London, he followed an unusual path to the top, serving as president of the prestigious Tsinghua University before becoming minister of environmental protection in 2015. As mayor of Beijing from 2017 to 2022, he played an important role in cleaning up the city’s notoriously polluted air.

Publicly, Chen has been loyal to Xi, so why was he purged? My guess is that Xi has become increasingly paranoid about the emergence of potential successors. Perhaps he heard one too many people praise Chen’s intelligence and management skills.

In a recent development, whatever the explanation, the purge points to a crisis in the CCP’s leadership. The question is whether that reflects genuine opposition to Xi or exists entirely in the leader’s imagination.

In a recent development, GOP’s Huang fallout. Republican Party pushback against Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has been surprisingly strong. Senators and influential figures such as Mitt Romney have come out against the decision and called for further investigation. Unless Trump intimidates them into submission, Nvidia could face scrutiny that may intensify once the fresh U.S. Congress takes office in January.

Huang is scheduled to testify publicly before Congress on Dec. 3, and even if Nvidia has seemingly secured a reprieve from federal investigation for now, it may have set itself up as an easy target for whatever presidential administration takes office in 2029.

It has been revealed that ‘Guaranteed bubble’ phenomenon. One aspect of the Nvidia scandal that has received little attention is how closely it resembles the way China treats private companies: protecting favorites and punishing those that fall out of favor. Trump has far less ability to intervene as freely as the CCP, but the parallels are worth noting.

In China, this kind of state interference helped create a phenomenon called the “guaranteed bubble.” The government has repeatedly stepped in to prop up companies when their troubles threaten to cause public unrest or economic insecurity. This created an expectation that these firms were too big to fail and therefore safe investments.

That confidence inflated the bubble further until reality caught up. Even if the artificial intelligence boom does not go that way, Trump’s interference threatens a long-standing U.S. advantage over China: trust that stock prices represent genuine value and that corporate failings are not being covered up by the state.

It has been revealed that robert Foyle Hunwick, a long-term China correspondent and a close friend of mine, died last week at 47 after a short battle with cancer. A British journalist who moved to China in the late 2000s, Rob wrote about society, crime, and nightlife in China and its neighbors for numerous outlets, including Foreign Policy.

Industry observers note that he loved both the humanity and the chaos of modern Chinese life and reserved some of his sharpest criticism for Western journalists who thought themselves above it all. He will be deeply missed.

Republicans, meanwhile, want to put together an emergency supplemental funding package with hundreds of billions of dollars dedicated to the military, munitions and war effort. DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN.

"Each side is a gamble," Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

He acknowledged that it was a give-and-take with Republicans, given that they do want up to $350 billion in emergency supplemental funding for the war and Pentagon, and that some limited agreements on guardrails for Iran war funding could be used as a bargaining chip for broader funding through the emergency package.

#202795. Latest Update: The Case for a Trump-Xi-Putin Summit
