But where more traditional Democrats believe this critique applies mostly to Republicans, many progressives would apply it with equal vehemence to Democratic foreign policy as well. And where one side largely believes that the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations tried, however imperfectly, to advance these goals amid a host of challenges, the other believes they could have done much more.

Sources indicate that A World for All, edited by Matt Duss (who previously served as a foreign-policy advisor to Sanders), bills itself as a “progressive blueprint” for U.S. foreign policy. It consists of 18 chapters, all written by different authors from the academic and think tank community covering a wide range of foreign-policy topics. At a time when a small but vocal group of Moscow apologists and Hamas enthusiasts has tried to put their stamp on the movement, this book shows that many thoughtful and principled voices still dominate progressive foreign-policy thinking. And as interest grows in the Democratic agenda after the midterms’ blue wave, it also serves as a welcome reminder of how much the entire party has in common when it comes to foreign policy.

Children wave flags and flowers as Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a ceremony in Beijing on May 20.Maxim Shemetov/China Pool via Getty Images.

In a recent development, russia, China, and the Middle East: If there are three areas where Washington struggles in pursuing peace, it is these. So what do the contributors to A World for All propose?

The greatest continuity appears in the case of Russia. Here, Michael Kimmage, a Cold War historian, suggests four pillars for U.S. policy:.

[M]aintaining and expanding meaningful channels of communication with Russia geared toward desired de-confliction and the avoidance of escalatory spirals; aiding Ukraine and containing Russian military power in Europe; monitoring Russia’s global activities and resisting them in a restrained and targeted, not reflexive or messianic fashion; and keeping an open mind as to Russia’s future.

It is hard to imagine most Biden officials finding anything here to disagree with. In fact, they might only object to the extent that this framing implies Biden himself was being reflexive, messianic, or close minded about Russia’s future.

The reason for this congruity, of course, is that the biggest obstacle to a cooperative relationship with Russia is Russia itself. As Kimmage writes, Washington “has been unable to find an enduring partnership, and it has been repeatedly surprised by aggressive Russian acts, from the invasion of Georgia in 2008 to the massive invasion of Ukraine in 2022.”.

In a recent development, he might have added that U.S. President George W. Bush initially sought to work with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the so-called war on terror, or that Obama came into office in search of his famous “reset” with Russia. But because of Russia’s actions, even progressives are now considerably more pessimistic about the possibility of a better relationship with Moscow than both their Republican and Democratic predecessors.

In the case of China, think-tankers Jake Werner and Sandy Shan offer a more pointed contrast with Biden’s approach. With the aim of building a more cooperative relationship with Beijing, they call for the next administration to “[s]et a course to ending economic warfare against China” and normalizing “the presence of China in the US economy.” The two powers, they argue, must work together to “reform global economic governance” and “advance global climate action.”.

Call them the restrainers, the riders, and the racers.

Meet the potential foreign-policy and national security major hitters of the next Congress.

The difference in their recommendations appears less in the stated goals than in what compromises a fresh president might make to achieve them. In responding to previous progressive critiques along the same lines, several former Biden officials have insisted that they too sought a cooperative relationship, but the problem came from Beijing. For example, Thomas Wright, who was on Biden’s National Security Council, argued in the Atlantic in July:.

Biden did seek to cooperate with China on issues of mutual concern, such as AI. But he insisted that this had to be done without preconditions. That’s because those of us who worked on these policies inside the administration knew the Chinese playbook well. Beijing had little interest in cooperating on climate or anything else. It would stall by demanding that the U.S. make a concession on some matter of strategic importance, such as Taiwan and export controls.

Recent findings suggest that while export controls or other economic measures might not be a concern for Werner and Shan, it is harder to tell how they think progressives should respond to demands for concessions on issues such as Taiwan. Here A World for All seeks to telegraph a different approach without necessarily spelling out the details.

Werner and Shan write that Chinese aggression against Taiwan would be a “cataclysm.” They argue that U.S. “measures to deter Chinese adventurism should therefore continue” but also be “balanced by stronger and more sincere efforts to reas­sure China that the United States is not pursuing permanent sepa­ration.” That is the sole reference to deterring Beijing in the book—which, read alongside repeated criticisms of U.S. militarism and the size of the Pentagon budget, certainly suggests a greatly reduced willingness to go to war in defense of Taiwan. And yet at face value, that line inevitably implies some commitment to using force. The result is nothing if not strategic ambiguity.

Industry observers note that needless to say, it is in the Middle East that the break with traditional Democratic foreign policy is clearest. The Biden administration’s consistent support for Israel’s genocidal policies in Gaza produced the starkest and most emotional division in the party. In the book, analysts Thanassis Cambanis and Zaha Hassan call for Washington to “end blank-check military support for Israel,” which increasingly seems like a demand that Democrats will make of any candidate in 2028.

Elsewhere in this section, though, their recommendations differ from past Democratic administrations more in degree than kind. They call for more diplomacy and fewer reckless wars, as well as supporting human rights over friendly autocrats. More pointedly, they call for reducing Washington’s military footprint in the region to “discourage unreliable partners and allies from starting wars they believe the US will finish for them.”.

U.S. Army soldiers watch as Barack Obama is sworn in as the 44th president of the United States at a base near Baghdad on Jan. 20, 2009.Chris Hondros/Getty Images.

Rhetorically, at least, these are all ambitions Obama and Biden shared. Obama ran on his opposition to the Iraq War, withdrew U.S. troops from Iraq, and resisted strong pressure to intervene in Syria. He also offered conditional support for the Arab Spring and negotiated a nuclear agreement with Iran, which he hoped would facilitate a “pivot to Asia.” Biden, for his part, campaigned on the promise to restore the Iran deal and make Saudi Arabia “a pariah” for its human rights abuses.

Recent findings suggest that both men, however, faced constraints in achieving these ambitions. Obama could have done more to push back against the military coup that ended any hope of a democratic transition in Egypt, but this was unlikely to change the ultimate outcome. In a similar vein, Obama was forced to send U.S. troops back to Iraq when the Islamic State upended the region, while Biden ultimately concluded that a fist bump with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was the price to pay for the cooperation on oil prices he needed to keep his domestic agenda on track.

It has been revealed that A more progressive administration is likely to face some of the same contradictions as their predecessors, even if they ultimately resolve them differently. Indeed, the challenge in evaluating this genre of policy writing, progressive or otherwise, is that, in the abstract, everyone wants their strategy to do everything. Whether you propose competing with rival powers while seeking areas of cooperation where possible or, alternatively, pursuing cooperation while competing where necessary, the real differences only emerge in the way policymakers negotiate the inevitable tradeoffs.

Of course, a constructive conversation about the tradeoffs Biden faced would be easier if members of his administration were more candid about where they fell short. So long as former officials continue to defend their record on Gaza, or proffer weak, equivocal, and mealy mouthed apologies, they will only make it harder to draw useful lessons from his tenure in other areas.

U.S. President Joe Biden (left) is welcomed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 15, 2022. Royal Court of Saudi Arabia/via Getty Images.

More broadly, A World for All suggests that progressives, no less than other Democrats, are still struggling with two enduring tensions that will plague any future administration.

Recent findings suggest that first, it is clear to everyone in the party that the health of U.S. democracy is intertwined with the fate of democracy worldwide. Yet the last few decades have also made it clear how limited Washington’s tools for democracy promotion can be. One approach that several authors highlight is a renewed focus on fighting corruption at home and abroad.

Industry observers note that progressives have led the way in insisting that authoritarianism and corruption are inextricably intertwined. A war against kleptocracy would be smart policy and smart politics, and it would certainly represent a concrete step toward making the world safe for democracy. Yet for the same reason, its impact would be limited so long as many of the countries the United States deals with remain authoritarian. Deploying Magnitsky sanctions against corrupt leaders implicated in bribing Americans or facilitating transnational repression is, in itself, an excellent idea. But it is also hard to imagine rebuilding ties with a newly introduced Russian government or pursuing a more cooperative relationship with China while simultaneously sanctioning some of their top officials.

U.S. President Donald Trump walks to Marine One at the White House in Washington on Oct. 6.Finn Gomez/Getty Images.

It has been revealed that the bigger contradiction is that in the very areas where both the traditional Democratic and progressive approaches to foreign policy differ from those of many Republicans—that is, diplomacy, cooperation, and multilateralism—they are uniquely susceptible to the kind of disruption Donald Trump has created. These all depend on trust and continuity, which is exactly what no one should expect from U.S. foreign policy in the coming decades. Among the many challenges Biden faced in restoring the Iran nuclear deal, for example, was Tehran’s demand for some reassurance that Trump would not simply tear it up again if he was reelected. This, of course, was something Biden could not provide and, as events proved, something that Iran was wise to ask for.

It has been revealed that in their chapter on Europe, analysts Rachel Rizzo and Max Bergmann offer one clear-eyed example of what confronting this reality could look like. They argue that, rather than simply try to restore the traditional transatlantic relationship rooted in a strong U.S. commitment to NATO, the next administration should support Europe’s efforts to become “a stronger and more assertive global actor” with more independent defense capabilities.

Can Washington hope to find actors abroad who will support U.S. values more reliably than the United States itself? It’s hardly an ideal solution. But then, if Democrats win the presidency in 2028, they will hardly be inheriting an ideal foreign policy situation.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • Sources indicate that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

Industry observers note that in June 2026, Google and Voltus unveiled a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

Sources indicate that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

Sources indicate that utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

It has been revealed that beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Recent findings suggest that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Industry observers note that wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

Industry observers note that bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

Eleven months after the law took effect — allowing Minnesota workers up to 12 weeks a year off with partial pay to care for a newborn or a sick family member, and up to 12 weeks to recover from their own serious illness — almost one in four Minneapolis city employees has used the benefit, the Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

Industry observers note that was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too big to fail”?

Jensen Huang was reinstated this week as CEO of Nvidia, a semiconductor manufacturer that’s a linchpin of the global artificial intelligence economy. That occurred only after U.S. President Donald Trump personally intervened to persuade Nvidia’s board—despite allegations that Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and his efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China in contravention of U.S. policy, may have undermined U.S. national security.

It has been revealed that was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley or D.C. elites? What levers did Trump use to pressure Nvidia’s board? Does Huang, or Nvidia more generally, qualify as “too massive to fail”?

It has been revealed that those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Recent findings suggest that cameron Abadi: Was Huang’s reinstatement initiated by Silicon Valley tech elites or by D.C. political elites—or an entwinement between the two?

Industry observers note that adam Tooze: Some reporting suggests that the rally around Huang really began in Silicon Valley itself. So it was a key group of people who were close to him: Uber founder Travis Kalanick, a bunch of venture capitalists like Gavin Baker, who’s been tweeting very effusively about this, Brad Gerstner and Marc Andreessen, who we’ve discussed on the show before. Heavy hitters. Apparently, there’s some Goldman Sachs interest as well. None of those people have really been willing to comment. But there was a rallying around Jensen Huang and the need to bring him back in. I think, basically, it was a combination of their influence plus a sell-off in the market that really prompted Trump to act. The venture capitalists have good connections to [Vice President] J.D. Vance, because he had that little foray in Silicon Valley finance by way of Peter Thiel. And they seem to then have been able to act on figures inside the Trump administration. Jensen Huang is, after all, very well known to Trump. The two have been seen together a lot in public.

Industry observers note that and then there was some last-minute fig leaf-style conversations with the attorney general just to confirm that they’re not actually supporting a figure that is at the moment under investigation by the American judicial authorities. So apparently the attorney general, Todd Blanche, signed off on this. And that was really then the decisive moment when Trump then intervened with the board, which seems to be a remarkably weak institution. For a organization of Nvidia’s size and significance, its corporate governance is schoolyard. It comes out of the era when it was a scrappy manufacturer of accelerator chips for video games rather than the biggest company in the world and the backstop to AI. So it seems to just be this incredible kind of jury-rigged, duct tape—you know, people refer to duct-tape empire—kind of setup that we’re dealing with here. And truly dramatic in its impact then on the market, though questions are being asked, I think, about how long the rebound can really last given the underlying questions about AI and the broader economy.

CA: What are the mechanics by which a leader of the U.S. government overrides a corporate board? And are there any precedents for a U.S. president personally intervening in a boardroom decision like this?

AT: I don’t think he has very many direct levers, other than his public sway. As corporate America has demonstrated across the board during his second term, no one wants to be on his wrong side. So if he told this weak corporate governance body at Nvidia that, you know, this is the way to go, and there really were no legal objections, at least at the level of espionage, then presumably they felt it was in the shareholders’ best interest to just do as they were told. It’s not entirely without precedent.

The most recent instance would be the Obama administration’s move against the leadership of General Motors in the spring of 2009 when the federal government did a bailout for General Motors. And they removed Rick Wagoner, who they didn’t feel that they could work with. Then beyond that, you have to go further back in history to the Cold War-era presidencies. So there’s action by the [Franklin] Roosevelt administration against the Ford Motor Tech giant leadership when they were deeply worried during the wartime about the succession of Henry Ford and deaths within the Ford family. There’s Truman intervening in the steel industry in the early 1950s. There’s a moment when Kennedy also intervenes at U.S. Steel in ’62.

Recent findings suggest that but, you know, the fundamental difference here is that we’re not in a state of war. This is not a matter of urgent national security or of macroeconomic pressure like in the early 1950s during the Korean War. This isn’t the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. Nvidia is not on the receiving end of a federal government bailout. You know, the analogies quite rapidly break down and leave one feeling that in some senses, this truly is an unprecedented intervention. This is the most valuable manufacturer in the world at various points. And it just basically doesn’t appear to have any serious corporate governance whatsoever.

Jensen Huang and the broader AI sector represent an enormous risk for the entire public.

The return of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang exposes a dangerous gap in corporate oversight.

CA: The intervention on behalf of Jensen Huang seemed to be motivated by a sense that he was somehow essential, not only to the success of the company, but through the company, to the success of the American economy overall. In what sense could Huang be considered to be “too big to fail”?

AT: Well, that term comes out of banking. And within the banking sector, since the Dodd-Frank reforms and other global financial stability reforms in the aftermath of 2008, designations as GSIB, so globally systemically significant banks and financial institutions, are formalized and have been formalized. And they do actually have a relatively formal or quantitative definition. I mean, you can look at bank balance sheets and just trace networks of interconnection and risks that arise from those. And there’s a quite serious study of those kinds of risks. And one could do the same for Nvidia. And there has been a great deal of speculation along these lines, or not just speculation, but investigation. And it’s quite clear that the circular financing mechanisms that we’ve also discussed on the show going back awhile now all center on Nvidia. And so questions have been asked about the stability of the Nvidia financing structure.

Industry observers note that but I think the question was always, should they not be subject to some kind of oversight? Right now, there is no risk of failure, right? In some senses this invocation of failure in the worst-case scenario—you know, she’s a spy and Nvidia is going to fail and therefore, you know, we must do x or y, or not do x or y, or bring him back or shove him out or whatever—the whole discourse is massively exaggerated. I mean, they’re a very successful tech business, which right now is in the middle of a boom in AI, which does have some bubble characteristics. But the financing of this is extended and ramified, but it’s the cloud providers, not necessarily Nvidia, that anyone thought of as being immediately in trouble. And even those are some way away from outright failure. And so this, you know, this language of exigency and this language of crisis, you know, it has a historical root and there are some structural reasons why one might worry about Nvidia, but it doesn’t justify the current action one way or the other. And the fact that the firm is as poorly structured as it is such that so much revolves around one man is prima-facie reason for, you know, some serious rethinking and some serious structural governance.

But that would require market pressure. And you know, the financial markets right now are bonkers. That they would reprice the tech giant by 30 percent of a trillion dollars on the basis of this kind of news is, in itself, you know, profoundly delegitimizing. So to my mind, like, it’s an absolute disaster of American public discourse, because the allegations appear to be hugely exaggerated, the damage done to the market suggests that the corporate governance is terrible, the reporting by the American media has been shambolic, the president’s intervention is unprecedented and bonkers, and now the markets vindicate the whole thing by raising the value of Nvidia by 30 percent. I mean, it feels like everyone’s kind of lost their minds in some ways. And yet, as someone famously noted, whilst the music plays, you dance. Because if you’re not on the Nvidia train, you’re not doing as well as other people. And all of these boosters are saying this is a vindication of the American success story and Jensen Huang is the latest character in that ongoing narrative. It all feels a bit delirious, to be honest.

#202756. America’s Hidden AI Advantage

America’s Hidden AI Advantage

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.
  • In a recent development, in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy.
  • It has been revealed that this narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JEFFREY DING is Assistant Professor of Political Science at George Washington University and the author of Technology and the Rise of Great Powers: How Diffusion Shapes Economic Competition.

The United States—Not China—Dominates Diffusion.

In a recent development, in the view of most observers, China is winning the race to diffuse artificial intelligence across the economy. Even if the United States has a small lead in frontier AI models, the consensus is that China is better at applying the technology. As Kevin Rudd, former prime minister of Australia and a prominent observer of Chinese politics, declared at a conference in October, China is “miles ahead” in spreading AI “into the real economy.” This fits a familiar narrative about the technological rivalry between the two great powers: the United States innovates while China turns those innovations into practical applications at scale.

It has been revealed that this narrative has become central to discussions of U.S.-Chinese competition in AI. But it doesn’t match reality. After the Chinese startup DeepSeek shocked the world in early 2025 with the announcement of an open-source large language model that rivaled the capabilities of frontier models made by American companies, the international media published breathless reports on how DeepSeek’s model had rapidly spread across state-owned enterprises, hospitals, and provincial and local governments. Months later, however, analysts determined that this adoption was shallow, narrow, and slow; the technology was being used on clunky “all-in-one machines” embedded on isolated hardware units within these institutions, rather than integrated more broadly into the software services they were using. Then, in January 2026, outside observers marveled at OpenClaw, a latest open-source AI agent, as a sign of China’s diffusion advantage. Now, the excitement about these open-source agents has dissipated as security vulnerabilities and inefficiency have limited their uptake.

According to recent reports, it is the United States, not China, that has a decisive lead in AI diffusion. This is because the United States has comparative advantages in both its overall level of economic development and the nature of its growth model. China’s underdeveloped software market, weak technology transfer mechanisms, and centralized economic system make AI diffusion much more challenging. All told, the United States’ advantage in diffusing the technology through the economy is likely to persist for the foreseeable future.

Despite its reputation as a pioneer of digital technology such as cashless payments and messaging apps, China’s overall digitization levels—the extent to which software and other digital tools have penetrated various sectors of the economy—are far lower than those in the United States. American firms are on average more than twice as likely as their Chinese competitors to adopt cloud computing services. And the U.S. enterprise software market, which includes services to manage customer relationships and provide business intelligence, is approximately ten times larger than China’s. According to the 2022 Global Cloud Ecosystem Index, which ranked 76 countries on their access to and usage of cloud services, China sat in the bottom half; the United States, by contrast, ranked 17th, not far behind the top performers, in part because of its dominance of “software as a service” products in which businesses can gain access to enterprise software without needing to install and maintain the programs themselves.

According to recent reports, china’s relatively low penetration of digital services is a barrier to diffusing AI. When small Chinese hospitals tried to adopt DeepSeek, for instance, they lacked information systems that could collect and manage the data necessary to take full advantage of AI models. In these hospitals, which include many small health facilities in rural areas, patient data is still recorded on paper; where digital records do exist, they are often incomplete or vary from hospital to hospital. By contrast, 95 percent of U.S. doctors maintain electronic health record systems in their offices. As a result, U.S. hospitals have more smoothly integrated AI into electronic health records to recommend treatments, predict health risks, and simplify billing.

China’s underdeveloped cloud and enterprise software ecosystem also explains why the OpenClaw hype did not translate to sustainable diffusion. Open-source tools like OpenClaw appeal to hobbyists and individual developers who are keen to experiment and are less sensitive to security issues. But small businesses have been slow to adopt such tools because they prefer reliable, standardized solutions that are easy to implement and upgrade. Small businesses are more likely to rely on cloud-based tools and enterprise software to implement AI upgrades than to try to experiment on their own—two channels that are less robust in China than in the United States.

Recent findings suggest that the United States also has an advantage over China because of linkages within the science and technology ecosystem that help disseminate advances. Collaboration between universities and businesses is critical to diffusing AI breakthroughs across the entire economy because these connections bring together innovators who can develop upcoming AI products and implementers who can effectively commercialize them.

According to recent reports, in this dimension, the United States is far ahead of China. Americans have long led the world in the publication of articles about AI co-authored by at least one researcher from academia and one researcher from industry. Between 2015 and 2019, U.S. researchers published more than twice as many such articles as their Chinese counterparts. The gap extends beyond AI: across the life sciences and natural sciences, the share of publications in the United States that involved both university and industry researchers was also more than double the comparable rate in China. Beijing recognizes this gap: China’s official state news agency ranked weak technical exchanges between industry and academia as one of the five crucial shortcomings of the country’s AI ecosystem.

In a recent development, although Chinese policymakers are aware of this challenge and have promoted policies to try to spur collaboration between universities and businesses, especially in AI, it will be difficult to cultivate the requisite trust needed for these two sectors to work together. China’s weak intellectual property protections, for example, discourage universities from pursuing partnerships with industry actors because they fear losing ownership of their inventions. The United States, by contrast, has a tradition of university-industry collaboration. The 1980 Bayh-Dole Act, which provides incentives and patent protections that encourage universities to commercialize inventions and license them to the private sector, kick-started decades of collaboration. Without a similar connective tissue to link academic institutions and businesses, Chinese universities are not as equipped to form profitable partnerships with companies. Chinese technical and engineering education is also disconnected from commercial enterprises, meaning that schools do not teach students the specific skills that companies need in their workforces.

Weak technology transfer mechanisms also undermine one of China’s main strengths in AI diffusion: its massive talent base. Analysis by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation showed that in 2022, China awarded around 50,000 doctoral degrees in science, technology, engineering, and math, compared with only about 34,000 in the United States. Although the sheer quantity of Chinese computer science graduates may eventually help the country adopt AI advances at scale, the quality of that education determines how rapidly or effectively education can encourage AI diffusion. If training is divorced from practical applications, graduates will struggle to adapt cutting-edge advances from industry labs into the sectors in which they work. Consider one commonly used standard to measure the baseline quality of AI education: whether a university employs at least one researcher who has published at least one paper at a leading AI conference. According to data from 2023–24, only 38 universities in China met this standard; the United States accounted for 150.

China’s centrally planned approach to AI development is also counterproductive when it comes to diffusion. In 2025, China developed an “AI Plus” action plan that outlines targets for AI adoption over the next decade and released guidelines for government agencies and local officials on how to put the plan into effect across the country. For many observers, the mere existence of a plan showed that the highest levels of Chinese leadership were committed to spreading AI widely and that China was better positioned to win the AI race than the United States, which lacks any kind of similar diffusion blueprint. Rudd’s claims about China’s edge in AI adoption, for instance, cite Beijing’s ambitious policies and targets for AI diffusion as supporting evidence.

But centralized approaches such as China’s often impede technology diffusion, especially when the state tries to intervene in domains in which the development trajectory is uncertain. One of the planks of China’s AI Plus blueprint identifies “global cooperation” as a priority sector for AI adoption. If local governments were to implement the plan as outlined, it would shift resources from areas in which diffusion has been proven to be effective, such as health care, to the undefined space of “global cooperation.” More broadly, Beijing’s favoritism toward state-owned enterprises and its preference for picking national champions often prop up inefficient technologies that would have been weeded out by market-based competition. Other businesses are unlikely to adopt inefficient technologies, making nonmarket forms of AI development less likely to diffuse widely.

According to recent reports, counterintuitively, the lack of a clear U.S. policy on AI diffusion is a boon, not a hindrance, to the United States’ attempt to diffuse the technology across the economy. At the height of U.S.-Japanese competition in the 1980s, for instance, when the two countries were racing to train software engineers who could spread computer technology, Japan’s Ministry of Education, Science, and Culture, as it was then known, exercised centralized control over universities. But emerging trends in computer science developed faster than the government could adapt. By concentrating state funds on centers of excellence and imposing one-size-fits-all rules on the computing curriculum, Japan could not match the adaptability of American universities, and the United States surged ahead. Cross-national studies have shown that decentralized science and technology systems are correlated with faster diffusion of upcoming innovations.

Another historical case with parallels to China, the Soviet Union, further suggests how centralization is antithetical to diffusion. In the twentieth century, the Soviet Union boasted many aims for technology development. Yet its top-down approach, which focused on large-scale engineering projects, undercut market-based instruments that encourage technology diffusion through competition. As a result, although the Soviet Union pioneered fresh technologies in many areas, including the casting of steel, it fell behind the United States in adopting general-purpose technologies such as computers. A prescient U.S. intelligence report published in 1969 deemed the Soviet Union’s mechanisms for technology diffusion as “much more balky” than those of the United States because of the absence of competitive pressures as well as limited linkages between the R & D system and the broader economy.

The myth of China’s lead in AI diffusion persists despite clear data showing U.S. advantages. In part, this may be because China’s innovation system has facilitated the widespread adoption of certain visible technologies. In less than 20 years, China has built more than 30,000 miles of high-speed rail, for example, blanketing the country with ultra-fast trains that now reach even the most remote provinces.

Recent findings suggest that but infrastructure presents a very different challenge than AI does. The centralized pressure that officials can use to effectively develop large-scale infrastructure projects is much less effective for general-purpose technologies like AI because it is infeasible to mandate that all small- and medium-size firms, spread across every sector of the economy, adopt artificial intelligence. Those companies would do so only if it made sense from a business perspective, and few have the digital foundations or savvy employees able to harness AI in a way that would help them grow. Moreover, the United States has outbuilt China in the infrastructure most essential to AI development, data centers, in which it retains a ten-to-one edge. In fact, in some cases, the data centers that China has built remain idle because of weak AI demand.

The misperception that China leads AI diffusion may continue unabated because analysis of the country’s technology ecosystem is overly focused on frontier firms such as ByteDance and DeepSeek and first-tier cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai. Yet AI diffusion ultimately rests on whether adoption occurs in medium size companies, small towns, and inland provinces, where it has been extremely limited. Because these settings rarely feature in outside media coverage, analysis of China’s AI diffusion landscape underestimates the difficulty of translating cutting-edge advances from frontier labs and universities in Hangzhou or Shenzhen to, say, a small firm in a county seat in northwestern Qinghai Province.

Perhaps the simplest explanation is that such a myth is useful, even if ultimately untrue. In some ways, the United States is trumpeting Beijing’s AI diffusion in the way that Chinese “tiger parents” try to motivate their children to work harder by raising the success of “that other family’s kid.” “Look at how well that other family’s kid performed at the piano recital,” they might say, without listening closely to ensure that the notes were exactly right. In great-power rivalry, too, there is a natural tendency to overhype the other side’s capabilities, in part to spur more effort at home.

It has been revealed that but such a “useful” myth can backfire if it pushes the United States to overlook its own advantages or even to mimic China’s more top-down approach to AI development. By any measure, the United States maintains a comfortable lead in AI diffusion, and China, despite its impressive successes, has serious challenges. Although the narrative of Chinese dominance endures, for now all signs point to a U.S. lead that will remain strong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘The Five’ weighs in on Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia following an affair scandal and his admission to additional affairs. The panel examines Democrats’ response, his welcome back to the firm and questions about potential national security implications.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance helped bring Jensen Huang back to the helm of Nvidia — a move that has reportedly exposed divisions within the administration and prompted one expert to warn it is "sending the wrong message.".

Recent findings suggest that the push to get Huang his job back has reportedly put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at odds with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the handling of national-security concerns involving Huang’s relationship with a woman whose alleged ties to Chinese intelligence remain in dispute, as well as questions about advanced U.S. chips reaching China.

According to recent reports, vance reportedly worked with Nvidia's board over the weekend to get Huang his job back, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who reportedly warned Trump about intelligence concerning the relationship, took another approach. Rubio has not publicly weighed in on the CEO's reinstatement and his office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The Vice President told CNN on Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche assured him that Huang was not under investigation.

"But most importantly, at just, I think, a personal level, we received the assurances that he was not under any significant, he was under no investigation, and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," he stated.

Vance continued, saying that he didn't think it was appropriate anyone should lose their job "because anonymous sources accuse them of things in the New York Times.".

The Nvidia saga reveals a "definitively split approach within the administration" toward China, as the manufacturer pressed for looser export controls, Max Meizlish of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies told Fox News Digital.

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent, left, and Secretary of Commerce nominee Howard Lutnick, speaks to the press as he signs an executive order to create a US sovereign wealth fund, in the Oval Office of the White House on February 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images).

TRUMP DEFENDS JENSEN HUANG'S CREDIBILITY, NVIDIA'S FUTURE AFTER BOARD REINSTATED CEO, INDICATES 'SEX SELLS'.

Nvidia said it received assurances from senior officials that Huang's reinstatement posed no national-security risk. But federal investigations were still underway into the Nvidia CEO's affair with a suspected Chinese spy and potential diversion of advanced U.S. chips to China when the president began his push.

The decision to reinstate Huang has left Republican lawmakers demanding to know what senior administration officials told Nvidia’s board that led them to reverse course less than two weeks after Huang's resignation.

The scrutiny intensified Monday when the Commerce Department added Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech giant tied to Huang’s former affair partner, to its trade blacklist after months of reported disagreement inside the administration over restricting the firm under investigation for allegedly helping divert Nvidia chips to the CCP.

Director of National Intelligence (DNI) Jay Clayton, however, said Sunday that investigations into Megaspeed and executive Alice Huang were ongoing, urging officials to "let that investigation play out" and "gather the facts.".

Trump stated Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the U.S. government had no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed the Trump administration to ease restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to China, making the company’s technology a focal point in the U.S.-China race for AI leadership. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, but when asked Monday night whether Huang had been cleared of national-security concerns or violations of federal law, Blanche declined to say. He argued that the question assumed facts about what the DOJ was investigating and claimed "a lot of thoughtful process by administration officials" went into the decision to back restoring Huang.

TWO TOP TRUMP CABINET OFFICIALS GO TO WAR OVER CHINA SPY SCANDAL AMID EXPLOSIVE ACCUSATIONS: REPORT.

Meizlish questioned the administration’s commitment to preventing chip diversion and told Fox News Digital that restoring Huang "is clearly sending the wrong message.".

"The company itself certainly has a lot of questions to answer," he added.

Recent findings suggest that alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, is under scrutiny over alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed is being investigated over possible diversion of advanced chips to China.

Bessent said Nov. 13 that Treasury, the State Department, the Pentagon and the U.S. Trade Representative had "for months" supported adding Megaspeed to the Entity List, but conceded that "Commerce has the pen" to decide whether to take action.

Recent findings suggest that bessent stated his deputy had been pushing for action. Prior reporting indicates Commerce officials resisted the move while other administration officials pressed for restrictions. Trump later acknowledged that Lutnick may have delayed action to avoid a "blowup with China.".

Treasury did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment and Commerce did not respond when asked about reports the department dragged its feet on implementing export controls on Megaspeed.

JENSEN HUANG IS BACK. NVIDIA’S BOARD STILL OWES AMERICA ANSWERS.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump speaks as Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio look on during a news briefing in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images).

Republican lawmakers are pressing for answers about what the administration knew before Nvidia’s board decided to bring Huang back.

Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, wrote on X: "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?".

Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., called Huang’s reinstatement a "mistake," warning it could "whitewash" unresolved national-security questions.

Industry observers note that the Republican chairmen of the House committees on Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and China said the board’s "brief internal investigation and reinstatement" did not erase the threats and questions they are investigating. Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter are scheduled to appear for transcribed interviews with the committees Dec. 1 and Dec. 2.

The congressional scrutiny comes amid separate questions about why it took months to blacklist Megaspeed and whether the controls now in place go far enough.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS.

Commerce added Megaspeed and six affiliates to the Entity List Monday, the same day Nvidia unveiled Huang’s return. The designation requires licenses for covered exports to the companies, with applications subject to a presumption of denial.

Sources indicate that "Commerce will continue to vigorously enforce export controls, including these new Entity Listings," the department mentioned. It explained the listing makes it unlawful to export U.S.-origin goods, software or technology to Megaspeed, and that advanced SI chips are also barred even when made overseas.

The scope of the controls is disputed.

Former National Security Council official Chris McGuire criticized Commerce for not applying an entity-specific foreign-produced direct product rule, which can extend U.S. export controls to some foreign-made goods produced with U.S. technology. He mentioned that without it, less advanced AI chips and components made overseas — including Nvidia H20 chips and high-bandwidth memory — could still be shipped to Megaspeed.

A Commerce official pushed back on McGuire’s characterization, telling Fox News Digital an entity-specific FDPR was unnecessary because the existing Advanced Computing FDPR already places advanced SI chips destined anywhere in the world under U.S. export controls.

In a recent development, treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick prior to an event with President Donald Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook in the Oval Office of the White House on Aug. 6, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images).

NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED'.

It has been revealed that commerce’s on-the-record statement similarly said advanced SI chips are barred from Megaspeed even when made overseas. McGuire’s criticism focuses on what he indicates remains outside those rules, including less advanced chips and components.

Meizlish said resellers would still need a license to supply Megaspeed, with applications presumed denied.

In a recent development, applying the entity-specific FDPR, he said, could further restrict the company’s access to foreign-made chips and components. Commerce did not specify whether H20 chips or the other components McGuire cited are covered by the existing rules.

It has been revealed that the White House maintains that its policy has been consistent, with spokesman Matthew Middleton telling Fox News Digital that "America’s most advanced chips must go to U.S. SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.".

A White House official also stated Trump has repeatedly ruled out allowing China to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced Blackwell and Rubin chips, and noted that Megaspeed has been under federal investigation since 2024 and Nvidia placed the company on its internal "no sell" list in June 2025.

The Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sent the organization's stock plunging, become a focus of internal and government investigations and is now threatening to reverberate across the AI industry. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, commerce said last week that the DOJ later took the lead in the criminal investigation. Neither department has confirmed charges against Megaspeed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more quickly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and new.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more rapidly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and fresh.

Industry observers note that each of the film’s two parts is just over two and a half hours long. The first, De Gaulle: Résistance (158 minutes; released in France as L’Age de fer), opens with the humiliation of the French collapse in June 1940. Refusing to accept the armistice, de Gaulle flees to England in a tiny plane. From there, he presses British Prime Minister Winston Churchill for greater support and builds a shaky government-in-exile from scratch, operating from a tiny office in central London.

The second, De Gaulle: Liberté (159 minutes; J’écris ton nom in France), covers 1943 to the end of 1944, following both the actions of the Resistance and de Gaulle’s power struggles with rival claimants to French leadership, before moving on to D-Day and the liberation of Paris. The epic closes movingly on Armistice Day, when Churchill visits the freed capital as de Gaulle’s guest.

For audiences outside France, some of this will be familiar, from de Gaulle’s defiant broadcasts on the BBC to his haughty and stubborn personal affect. Undeniably imperious and quite unable to forget a slight, Abkarian’s de Gaulle is both a model of determination in the face adversity and, to the Allied leaders who bankrolled him, a quintessentially French pain in the ass.

A still from De Gaulle: Résistance.Pathe Films.

In a recent development, other episodes are less well known in the English-speaking world, however, even as they remain central to France’s own story of the war, from the British destruction of the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in July 1940 (to keep its warships out of German hands) to the epic battle at Bir Hakeim in mid-1942. Perhaps now more familiar to tourists as the name of a Paris metro station, Bir Hakeim saw 3,700 Free French soldiers and their African colonial troops hold an isolated desert fort in Libya against German Gen. Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps for more than two weeks. Fighting against overwhelming odds, their bravery allowed Britain’s Eighth Army to fall back to El Alamein and regroup, marking an eventual turning point in the wider war. Providing the first film with a dramatic 15-minute denouement, the battle proved that de Gaulle’s ragtag movement could fight as a real army, provided a much-needed fillip to Free French morale, and strengthened the general’s position as a legitimate and potentially successful French leader.

According to recent reports, although this is very much a major-budget war movie, much of its power lies, paradoxically, in its intimate portrayal of the quiet complexities of leadership. In the public mind, de Gaulle can often come across as a cartoonish figure, all stubborn resolve, frosty self-regard, and Gallic hauteur. Abkarian’s ramrod-stiff performance is magnetic and provides plenty of evidence of this. But it also offers something more human, portraying with affection de Gaulle’s strange mix of grandeur and loneliness. The first film dwells in particular on his isolation and frequent despair. Arriving in London as a defeated tank division commander and former undersecretary of war, de Gaulle has no army, no money, barely any staff, and little claim to legitimate leadership. His situation is often tragi-comic, as when he tries unsuccessfully to win over members of the French expatriate community at a drinks party, or when he attempts to address a British audience in a packed theater, only to walk off ashamed without saying a word. In one especially memorable scene, he weeps alone in the bath of his small, dingy flat. In many others he is disconsolate, close to losing hope, and tempted to give up.

According to recent reports, this most Gallic of films is in fact based on an equally epic book by a British academic: A Certain Idea of France, Julian Jackson’s 900-page biography, published in 2018. Reviewing it in the New Yorker, Adam Gopnik dwelt on the crippling weakness de Gaulle faced in 1940, and how he ultimately managed to think his way out of it via a mixture of imagination, self-belief, and obstinacy. De Gaulle depended “more on theatrical élan than did pretty much any other public man of his century,” as Gopnik put it. “No one has ever played a weaker hand more compellingly. His life was one long brilliant bluff.”.

Sources indicate that it is this vulnerability, rather than the more familiar image of pigheaded strength, that likely appealed to French audiences, prompting a reassessment of his traditionally unbending image and the controversial Gaullist legacy it inspired. For all that, the film is also huge fun. Its action sequences are slickly executed and, unusually for a European production, come with plenty of exuberant, Hollywood-style explosions. But it works as entertainment above all because at its center is the double act of de Gaulle and Churchill, played by Simon Russell Beale, easily the best of the many actors who have attempted the role.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

The two men are endlessly frustrated by one another and an obvious study in contrasts: one reserved, austere, and abstemious, the other impulsive, theatrical, and alcoholic. Yet each recognizes in the other a wartime leader fighting to save his nation against massive odds, creating a certain fondness and clear mutual regard. Among their many fine scenes is a comic row involving translation. De Gaulle speaks poor English; Churchill’s French is comical but serviceable. As they argue, both men hear their respective interpreters diplomatically softening their words. Each leader throws his man out of the room in turn, preferring to fight out their differences in broken language. The grudging but sincere warmth between the two both humanizes the complexities of wartime leadership and provides the film’s emotional heart.

It has been revealed that some critics have accused director Baudry of playing fast and loose with history, mixing invented characters with historical leaders, among other sins against accuracy. Jackson, who acted as a consultant on the production, has written warmly in its defense: “My pavlovian historical pedantry – ‘no that is wrong, it didn’t happen like that’, ‘you have these events in the wrong order’, etc – was swiftly slapped down with the reminder that this was a film not a documentary.”.

According to recent reports, the film’s very French portrayal of the United States, with a Machiavellian President Franklin D. Roosevelt cast as a chief villain, is one obvious area of potential historical dispute. But it also provides the film with its drama. Curiously, Adolf Hitler is never seen and barely even mentioned, while few German soldiers even appear. Instead, the real antagonist is Roosevelt’s Washington, and the U.S. president’s mounting frustration with an upstart French exile who contributes little manpower to the war effort yet irritatingly demands to be treated as an equal and a great power. In this sense it has something in common with zombie movies, where the greatest danger often comes less from the outside menace and more from potential betrayal within the group of humans struggling to survive.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

In Roosevelt’s eyes, France had forfeited any claim to great-power status, while de Gaulle himself was merely an arrogant annoyance and obstacle to his aims. This broader threat to French survival is embodied in a initiative to create the Allied Military Government of Occupied Territories (AMGOT), which the film presents as a U.S. scheme to permanently dismantle and divide the country. In this vision, a liberated France would be run by U.S. and British administrators, much as occupied Germany later was. That AMGOT was never the fully formed plan for France the film suggests is almost beside the point. In one memorable scene, Churchill is shown a future map of Europe in which France has vanished, carved up into a “New Wallonia” and other invented entities. In an act of covert friendship, he leaks it to de Gaulle; a rare act of British solidarity with the French over the Americans.

Sources indicate that as exaggerated as the film’s version of the AMGOT plan may be—and Jackson concedes it is somewhat overplayed—the question of how to deal with a powerful United States runs throughout the film, giving it its most obvious modern resonance. In part this reflects a traditional and enduring Franco-British divide, with France seeking self-sufficiency and sovereignty while Britain prefers proximity and access to Washington.

To distract from runaway protests, the French president is making a show of independence on the world stage.

The film’s ideas have poisoned military thinking for centuries.

On the eve of D-Day in June 1944, for instance, de Gaulle’s demands over his forces’ role in the coming liberation of France prompt another giant bust-up with Churchill, and one especially memorable exchange, recounted in de Gaulle’s own highly readable memoirs. “”Every time we have to choose between Europe and the open seas, we shall always choose the open seas,”” he recalls Churchill declaring. “”Every time I have to choose between you and Roosevelt, I shall always choose Roosevelt.”” From Churchill’s point of view, this was entirely sensible; Britain had no obvious alternative to a superpower’s existential support, and it would have been foolish to side with an exile liberation army possessing no resources of its own. Nonetheless, it was a line de Gaulle would go on to quote throughout his life: an emblem of British perfidy and deference to Washington.

Late in the second film, in a scene set in November 1944, de Gaulle sounds out Churchill on a deeper Anglo-French alliance. Churchill declines because Britain must stay close to Washington. The portrayal feels both enduring but also clearly modern, depicting two exhausted European powers facing common adversity but still quite unable to choose to be full partners with one another.

In a recent development, more than anything, the film brings to mind the modern predicament of embattled and weakened middle powers, trying to find their way in a world dominated by far larger and more chaotic forces. During World War II, Britain and France both still thought of themselves as great powers—in de Gaulle’s case almost absurdly so, given his limited circumstances. Yet both clearly lived at the mercy of others, be they Hitler’s marauding armies or the caprice of an indispensable but overbearing U.S. ally.

Today European nations face a version of the same bind, struggling to rebuild sovereignty in a world dominated by superpowers increasingly willing to coerce and threaten them. The message of the film is clearly a comfortable one for French audiences: France was right all along about untrustworthy Americans, and about the need for strength and independence rather than reliance on potentially unreliable U.S.-led institutions like NATO. Nonetheless, here de Gaulle offers modern Europeans clear lessons on how to counteract weakness, via a mixture of political imagination, risk-taking, and—above all—a willingness to stand up to U.S. power from time to time.

Sources indicate that what most people understand as “Gaullist” policies are increasingly common far beyond France as our geopolitical order frays, not least intrusive industrial policies aimed at technological self-sufficiency. Ben Judah, a British author and former political advisor, has gone further, proposing a fresh agenda of “Anglo-Gaullism” inspired by the French leader’s mixture of interventionism and political élan. “[T]he genius of de Gaulle was to re-enchant through storytelling a nation that had utterly lost confidence in itself,” he writes. Europe could clearly use a little more of that Gaullist enchantment today.

Recent findings suggest that it is almost a cliche to contrast the giants of World War II with the slighter figures of our own generation. Yet watching de Gaulle’s struggles, it is hard not to think of the supplication of modern leaders like Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, whose approach to U.S. President Donald Trump was memorably described by Susan Glasser of the Upcoming Yorker as “strategic self-abasement.” De Gaulle is often fairly criticized for a grandiose vision of French leadership that far outstripped France’s actual power, leading to unhelpful delusions of national grandeur fed by the vision of its grandest of leaders. Nonetheless, de Gaulle’s obdurate refusal to accept decline—and his determination that France should stand, as he put it, as a nation “in the front rank”—should serve as an inspiration to Europe’s leaders today. This, too, is the lesson of the two excellent films that bear his name: to hold a vision of national power and to will it obstinately into existence, even if only by learning how to play a bad hand well.

In a recent development, james Crabtree is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a distinguished visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, and the author of The Perimeter: America's Struggle for Primacy in the Pacific (forthcoming in January) and The Billionaire Raj: A Journey Through India’s New Gilded Age. X: @jamescrabtree.
