Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side.
  • It has been revealed that the House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide mentioned on Tuesday.
  • It has been revealed that but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reps. Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

It has been revealed that the House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide mentioned on Tuesday. The bill, which passed the Senate on Nov. 19 in a 62-33 vote, has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and a wide range of industry groups that are generally GOP allies. Adoption of the rule, typically a party-line affair, would almost certainly lead to final passage and Trump's signature.

It has been revealed that but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in a Nov. 20 letter to colleagues, implored them to come back to work next month to finish out the lame-duck session, citing the permitting bill vote among other things. But it remains to be seen whether defeated lawmakers will take him up on that.

And several Republicans, led by House Freedom Caucus members, have used their leverage in rule votes to extract last-minute changes to legislation from leadership.

According to recent reports, last December, the House considered a bill to overhaul the National Environmental Policy Act from Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman, R-Ark. Ahead of the vote on that rule, Republicans including Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., sought last-minute changes to portions of the bill they were concerned would allow offshore wind projects in the Atlantic Ocean to move forward. Westerman agreed, which in turn caused the American Clean Power Association to withdraw support for the bill.

It has been revealed that harris hasn’t commented yet on the Senate-passed permitting measure. Nor has Freedom Caucus Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, who has called for permitting generally to be a lame-duck priority but was another one of the holdouts on Westerman’s bill last year. Still, the Freedom Caucus is generally on board with permitting legislation and specifically cited it as a priority for the session's waning days.

Industry observers note that republicans are generally expected to support the bill, which enjoys backing from industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, National Mining Association and Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities. The bill’s supporters go beyond the energy sector, including groups like the American Road and Transportation Builders Association and National Association of Home Builders.

And two Democrats — Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, both members of the Blue Dog Coalition — have taken the rare step of crossing the aisle to support Republican rules this year in order to move legislation they support. Both have issued statements that speak favorably of the permitting bill.

Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, one of the bill's lead authors, was enthusiastic about the bill's chances in the other chamber.

"I think there’s a real will there," the West Virginia Republican noted Tuesday after presiding over a pro forma session. "We’ve got to get enough Republicans there to vote, and I think that’s what the speaker is hoping to do. I think he wants to do it under a rule, it sounds like, but I’m very excited about it because I think it’s very, very doable.".

With the path through the House yet to be fully illuminated, a vote under suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds of members present and voting to pass, remains an option. But that's a trickier path given the split among Democrats.

The Senate-passed bill emerged from that chamber in a weaker position than advocates anticipated earlier this month, when 73 senators backed advancing it on an initial procedural vote.

After opponents got through with the measure — including an amendments blockade by Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden that left backers unable to incorporate changes necessary to shore up support — there were just 62 "yes" votes, although there were four absent GOP supporters.

Just 15 out of 47 Democratic caucus members voted for it, including only one member of the Environment and Public Works panel — Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, who wrote the bill with his GOP and Democratic counterparts on EPW and Energy and Natural Resources.

If there is full attendance on both sides, the threshold for passage on suspension would be about 290 votes. Permitting bill supporters would need about one-third of House Democrats to vote in favor — 71 with current vacancies — similar to their level of Senate Democratic support, assuming all Republicans were on board.

That doesn’t seem out of the question given that the leadership of the 112-member-strong Upcoming Democrat Coalition has expressed support led by the current chair, Brad Schneider of Illinois; the incoming chair, fellow Illinoisan Nikki Budzinski; and Scott Peters, D-Calif., chair of the coalition’s Environment, Climate and Clean Energy Working Group. So has the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.

In a recent development, clean energy groups like the Solar Energy Industries Association and American Clean Power Association back the bill, as do key labor unions including the AFL-CIO, Laborers’ International Union of North America and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL-CIO sent a legislative alert on the bill, which indicates it may include the measure on its annual legislative scorecard.

Recent findings suggest that but Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is a firm “no” on the current bill. He offered a series of changes on Monday needed to win his support — which have negligible chance of acceptance by the bill’s authors or by Trump, who last week said the bill would put money “back in the pockets of hardworking Americans” and lead to “tremendous amounts of new building.”.

It has been revealed that huffman wants to roll back proposed limits on Endangered Species Act reviews as well as the bill's 150-day limit on judicial challenges and “project certainty” protections intended to bar future administrations from revoking approved permits. Huffman remarked the certainty protection would legislate “a third term for Trump” by preventing future administrations from revoking permits for projects that could have detrimental environmental impacts, such as fossil fuel or mining projects.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the official position of the nearly 100-member Congressional Progressive Caucus is opposed. And the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition said it couldn’t support the Senate bill without changes, arguing the measure “includes environmental rollbacks that are concerning to us.”.

According to recent reports, two influential Democrats on energy and climate issues came out against the measure in its current form this week — Reps. Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin of California, who are among the SEEC’s vice chairs. Casten and Levin have worked together on legislation intended to overhaul the transmission permitting system and address energy affordability.

In a statement Casten stated the bill would make it “impossible” for a future administration “to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent,” adding he would vote "no" on the Senate-passed bill “with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”.

Casten, who co-founded a clean energy startup before coming to Congress, is currently challenging House Financial Services ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the gavel next year, in a bid resting in part on his environmental bona fides, including sustainable investment and climate-risk regulation.

Levin, an environmental lawyer by trade, praised the bill’s provisions making it easier to build interstate transmission lines, a key bottleneck barring the development of more wind and solar power generation.

“These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon,” Levin said in his statement. But he said it wasn’t worth the potential environmental costs, adding that “taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”.

Major environmental advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have long been opposed to the measure, as have Native American tribes and representative organizations like the National Congress of American Indians.

Another factor affecting the debate in the House is how to handle a bipartisan package of Senate changes agreed to on both sides of the aisle, but blocked on the floor by Merkley, a staunch opponent of the bill.

That amendment included language making it more difficult to circumvent National Historic Preservation Act rules; giving landowners and state regulators more time to resolve disputes before eminent domain is invoked for transmission projects; and closing loopholes in the bill’s language aimed at making data center developers pay for their own electric-grid upgrades.

According to recent reports, if that amendment had been included, the Senate vote count may have been higher. But attaching it in the House would send it back to the Senate for another round of votes, which may not be practical given the dwindling legislative session. An alternative would be to tuck the amendment into another must-pass bill, like government funding legislation or the National Defense Authorization Act.

The New Democrat Coalition’s statement, while overall supportive, said the group “will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns.”.

Senate Indian Affairs Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and ranking member Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, worked on changes in the amendment to address concerns tribes and Native American organizations raised about the NHPA section.

“I'm not going to abandon it just because the bill has been passed now. So working it on the House side, looking for other opportunities to advance it yet this Congress,” Murkowski said Nov. 20. “So we're not done.”.

Capito told reporters Tuesday that the permitting bill's fate has been invading her dreams.

Sources indicate that "My husband Charlie wakes me up, I’m like in sleep going ‘huh, huh, huh.’ He goes, ‘What’s wrong? What’s wrong?’ I mentioned, ‘I’m just dreaming about permitting reform,'" Capito recalled. "That’s kind of a sad state of affairs. It was our 50th anniversary.”.

Lauren Green, Jackie Wang and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#202751. Tech Report: The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1827 w)

Tech Report: The Model Middle Power

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America.
  • In the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent.
  • Industry observers note that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANDREW YEO is a Senior Fellow and SK-Korea Foundation Chair at the Brookings Institution and Professor of Politics at the Catholic University of America. This essay is adapted from his forthcoming book South Korea’s Grand Strategy: Narratives and the Rise of a Global Nation.

What South Korea Gets Right About Geopolitics.

In the ten months since Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave his widely discussed speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the question of whether, and how, the world’s middle powers can help rebuild a broken international order has become increasingly urgent. In his remarks, Carney stressed that although the old U.S.-led alliance system was collapsing, middle powers—states that do not have the ability to reshape global politics but that still possess substantial might—were well positioned to pick up the slack. But to do so, Carney argued, they would need to build up their “strength at home” and “act together” to harness their collective power, even in the absence of backing from the world’s hegemon.

Industry observers note that although the Canadian prime minister’s bold vision was widely applauded, some experts thought his agenda was overly ambitious. They noted, correctly, that it would be very difficult for middle powers to build a grand alliance composed of countries as diverse as Brazil, Canada, South Africa, and Turkey. “The path to unity among middle powers is fraught because this group includes rich and poor countries, as well as small and large ones,” wrote the economist Eswar Prasad in February. Carney, however, is right that middle powers have an opportunity to thrive going forward. Even when aligning with great powers, these countries can still exercise greater autonomy by developing national capacity and diversifying external partnerships.

Recent findings suggest that south Korea offers a prime example of this flexible approach. For decades, Seoul has pursued a middle-power strategy centered on building domestic strength and forging partnerships with democracies everywhere while deepening its alliance with Washington. South Korea has been adaptable, recalibrating its security alignments, economic strategies, and diplomatic roles as regional and global conditions require. This has enabled a country smaller in size than most of the world’s states to punch far above its weight, exercising substantial influence in Asia and beyond.

Not every government can follow Seoul’s path, and South Korea’s strategy has its limits. As Seoul itself acknowledges, middle powers cannot escape great-power competition. But the country has begun to show what middle powers can accomplish when they leverage their partnerships and their own strength to protect their interests and deter larger threats. And by maintaining and even building its ties to the United States while asserting greater autonomy, South Korea has proven that middle powers can strengthen themselves without building whole fresh networks—contrary to Carney’s suggestion.

Recent findings suggest that according to classic international relations theory, grand strategy is the exclusive provenance of great powers. The United States’s effort to contain the Soviet Union during the Cold War is a paradigmatic example; China’s pursuit of global economic primacy is another. Middle powers, by contrast, have little say in such strategies. Instead, these countries are seen as primarily reactive in their foreign policies, navigating around the decisions of the great powers rather than setting the agenda themselves.

Recent findings suggest that but recent history suggests that the division between great and middle powers is less clear-cut than has been assumed. In practice, middle powers very much have their own affirmative visions that they pursue in the world. They have the leeway to decide which threats matter most to them, which partnerships to prioritize, and where to invest scarce resources. Japan, concerned with the threat posed by China, has been quietly exercising leadership in the Indo-Pacific by improving its ties with neighbors, increasing investment and aid to the region, and strengthening its own defense capabilities—all while remaining closely allied with the United States. India, worried about China, Pakistan, and growing economic headwinds, has successfully bolstered partnerships with the United States and other democracies but maintained its relationship with Russia.

According to recent reports, much like Japan and India, South Korea is worried about its neighbors. But for Seoul, this is nothing new. South Korean leaders have been concerned with the very thing Carney fretted about in his Davos speech—becoming collateral damage in conflicts between great powers— since at least the late nineteenth century, when it was caught between China, Japan, and Russia. The country has a well-known proverb, “When whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken,” that captures the sentiment that great-power feuds can harm countries caught in the middle.

To safeguard against this threat, Seoul has long sought to increase its self-reliance through industrial policy. The country transited from light to heavy export industries in the 1970s, turning it into a major player in the chemical, steel, and shipbuilding sectors. State investments helped it become a major global producer of batteries and semiconductors in the present era. South Korea takes great pride in what historians call “the miracle on the Han”—or the country's rapid rise from a war-torn and impoverished state to a rich one during the late twentieth century. They now use the state’s wealth to promote public goods globally, contributing to international development, global health, climate policy, and multilateral bodies.

Recent findings suggest that seoul has also built up a formidable military, one that experts consistently rank as among the strongest in the world. Today, many South Korean analysts argue that Seoul needs a nuclear arsenal for self-defense, even though the country officially remains under Washington’s nuclear umbrella. The state has simultaneously used its armed prowess to deepen relations with U.S. allies. Seoul, for example, has inked multibillion-dollar arms deals with European buyers, making it a key partner in rebuilding NATO’s industrial capacity. In 2025, it was the second largest supplier of weapons to European NATO members (after the United States). South Korea has also forged defense partnerships in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, widening Seoul's options and reducing its dependence on any single market. South Korea, in other words, has been able to convert its economic resources and bureaucratic capabilities into greater influence by expanding its partnerships, strengthening its voice in international bodies, and helping shape global rules and norms.

But even as it charts its own path, Seoul has no intends to abandon the United States, at least in the near future. In fact, the sanctity of the U.S.-South Korean relationship is a significant historical Korean narrative. Many South Koreans see the alliance as a bond inked in blood, thanks to the sacrifice both countries made during the Korean War, when they worked to stop North Korea, backed by China and the Soviet Union, from overrunning the south. Most South Koreans correctly believe that the continued U.S. military presence in the country—currently, 28,500 American troops are stationed on the peninsula—has played a major part in deterring North Korean aggression over the past seven decades.

At first glance, South Korea’s strategy may seem contradictory. On the one hand, the country wants to deepen its cooperation with the United States, on which it still depends for security. But on the other, it seeks greater autonomy.

Yet these twin goals are not actually at odds. By cultivating ties with Washington, Seoul has gained access to advanced military capabilities and technologies as well as a larger diplomatic platform to expand its regional and global interests. It is in part because of this relationship, for example, that South Korea has had such success at selling weapons to multiple NATO members, including Croatia, Estonia, Finland, Norway, Poland, and Romania. (Seoul has also built up a formidable diplomatic apparatus in its own right.) At the same time, South Korea helps make this compact worthwhile for the United States by providing it with valuable technology, including semiconductor chips. Seoul has also partnered with the Washington to help revive the American shipbuilding industry, agreeing to invest $150 billion in the U.S. sector.

Still, South Korea’s growing push for more independence in its foreign policy does result in some tensions with the United States that cannot easily be resolved. For instance, the current government’s push to give Seoul, not Washington, operational control over both states’ forces on the peninsula in the event of war has been rebuffed by the U.S. military. American commanders instead favor a conditions-based transfer after South Korea has proven it has the capabilities to lead a joint defense, rather than setting a fixed date. The two sides also have not reached a consensus on what role South Korea would play if Taiwan is attacked or blockaded by China.

Recent findings suggest that yet so far, Seoul has done an effective job at managing these differences. For example, in his second term, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused Washington’s allies, including South Korea, of leeching off the United States and not paying their fair share. To extract more from Washington’s partners, Trump has implemented punishing tariffs. In response, South Korea could have been defiant and slapped on retaliatory restrictions, as other U.S. allies did. Instead, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung avoided rebuking the president and worked to meet American demands in ways that heightened the two states’ mutual dependence. For instance, Lee pledged to invest $350 billion in the United States to advance American economic and national security interests, including by purchasing more U.S. military equipment, and to increase South Korean economic support for locally stationed American forces.

It has been revealed that seoul’s strategy has not been a uniform success. The South Korean economy remains exposed to American and Chinese pressure despite its growth and diversification. North Korea is expanding its nuclear and missile forces and deepening military ties with Russia, creating new security headaches for which Seoul still needs U.S. assistance. The country is politically polarized, resulting in sharp policy shifts that can undermine long-term strategic planning. It also suffers from the lowest birthrate of any country in the world, threatening its tax base and the size of its armed forces. Beyond that, South Korea may not provide the ideal template for every middle power. Not every country in this category has similar economic resources, networks, or ties to the United States.

But on the whole, South Korea’s grand strategy has been effective, and it thus carries broader lessons. For one, it highlights how adaptive middle powers can draw on their respective national narratives to find their strengths and to chart a path forward. Perhaps more important, it is proof positive that middle powers can exercise influence and achieve a measure of autonomy even without working together to build a neutral third pole, as Carney urged. It also illustrates that middle powers can remain firmly allied with the United States while developing their own independent capabilities. South Korea, then, demonstrates that states can reduce their vulnerability and widen their political options.

ES Foundry, a U.S. manufacturer of high-efficiency solar cells, is at RE+ 2026 this week to showcase its American-made solar cells and announce a milestone in its operating capacity.

According to the manufacturer, it is the first and only crystalline silicon solar cell manufacturer to ship more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of domestically manufactured solar cells in the United States.

Sources indicate that as one of the few U.S. solar cell manufacturers with a fully operational facility producing and shipping cells to customers, ES Foundry is helping move American solar manufacturing to commercial reality.

In July, the company revealed it reached its full 3-GW manufacturing capacity. The company began production on its first 1-GW line last year and has now completed its 2-GW expansion line.

Solar Power World attended the opening of its Greenwood, South Carolina facility last year, reporting on its manufacturing outfit and its unique approach to supply deals that include working with large-scale project developers and utilities to guarantee domestic content supplies.

According to recent reports, at RE+, attendees can see its U.S.-manufactured high-efficiency monocrystalline bifacial PERC solar cells and meet with company representatives to discuss domestic sourcing, manufacturing capabilities, and the evolving needs of the U.S. solar market.

According to recent reports, “There’s an important difference between talking about building a domestic solar supply chain and actually making it happen,” mentioned ES Foundry CEO Alex Zhu in a statement. “At ES Foundry, we’re manufacturing at commercial scale, shipping cells to customers and navigating the realities of U.S. production every day. That experience gives us a unique perspective on what it will take to build a competitive, sustainable American solar industry. Success requires more than manufacturing capacity. It requires the right economics, technology investments, customer demand and policies to support long-term growth. We’re proud to be delivering on the promise of American manufacturing today while helping shape the industry’s future.”.

Visit ES Foundry at RE+ 2026: Booth C7434, November 16–19, Las Vegas, Nevada.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brendan Glavin, director of insights at the campaign finance research group OpenSecrets, explains why the GOP's cash advantage didn't translate to victories on Election Day.

Before polling began to show dire warning signs for the GOP ahead of the midterm elections, some in conservative circles felt they had a not-so-secret weapon that would give them an edge over their Democratic rivals — a massive amount of cash.

Across the Republican National Committee, Senate Leadership Fund, Congressional Leadership Fund, National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the GOP brought in roughly $1.7 billion in funds to fuel its ill-fated midterm campaigns.

The five equivalent Democratic committees, meanwhile, raised well over $300 million less than that total but walked away with massive pickups in even traditionally deep red strongholds like Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and Mississippi.

Experts from across the political spectrum explained this result to Fox News Digital by arguing that the impact of money on politics is less than what many in the public may assume and that massive fundraising hauls can only take a party so far when it faces political headwinds as strong as those weathered by the GOP in the run-up to election night.

MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE.

GOP electoral efforts were buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC. (Getty Images).

In a recent development, on top of their already significant nine-figure lead, GOP electoral efforts were also buoyed by a duo of PACs — President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk’s America PAC — which themselves collected an additional $665.4 million for Republicans to burn through. Despite such a massive financial edge, the GOP suffered one of its worst midterm performances in history, losing Senate seats even in deep red jurisdictions like South Carolina and Mississippi.

Still, Capital Research Center President Scott Walter, argues: "Money is not magic.".

According to recent reports, "Democrats should remember that when tempted to curtail political speech with donation limits, and Republicans should remember that when tempted to think more money automatically means more votes," the leader of the right-of-center group told Fox News Digital. "That will be news to those like Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., who thinks billionaires and ‘dark money’ control the cosmos.".

Walter pointed out, citing data aggregated by OpenSecrets, that the biggest donor in any given election cycle rarely ends up getting what they want out of the American political system.

Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at OpenSecrets, a nonprofit dedicated to tracking money in politics, told Fox News Digital that, while money certainly moves the needle in elections, its actual impact can be blunted by a variety of factors — many of which were at play during the recent midterms.

In a recent development, AI IS SUPERCHARGING POLITICAL AD WARS. BUT VIRAL DOESN’T MEAN VICTORIOUS.

Elon Musk presents a $1 million check during an America PAC town hall ahead of the Wisconsin Supreme Court election, in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on March 30, 2025. (Jamie Kelter Davis/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"​​Certainly, you know, the money makes a difference," said Glavin.

It has been revealed that "When both sides are engaging in a sort of arms race, right, and they're both spending almost equivalently, then really the effect is lost," he explained. "If you're somebody [who] sees an ad for one candidate, and then it's immediately followed by an ad for another candidate… essentially, you're not moving the needle.".

In many of the marquee races of Election Day, such as the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, both parties had enough money to saturate the airwaves with their messaging, potentially creating the environment described by Glavin.

Industry observers note that "This election was very unique," he told Fox News Digital. "What people probably really didn’t see until afterward is there was this significant headwind and voters were feeling a certain way and more ads were not going to change that.".

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL.

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the big SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," one expert said. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images).

Glavin, to support his argument, pointed to the fact that self-funding candidates running in elections often fail to make much headway, serving as evidence for the claim that ludicrous amounts of money don’t automatically equate to political success.

One of the most obvious recent examples is former Newly introduced York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg, who spent roughly $1.1 billion of his own money on his 2020 presidential campaign. He won only 55 delegates in the Democratic primaries at an approximate cost of $18 million per delegate.

Academics who spoke to Fox News Digital were divided on the impact money has on elections.

"Money has diminishing returns," Ray La Raja, a professor of political science at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told Fox News Digital. "And in [an] election wave environment where the president and his party is overwhelmingly disliked or distrusted, money can do little to save them.".

JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026.

Sources indicate that michael Bloomberg discusses his presidential run on Nov. 25, 2019, in Norfolk, Virginia. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

John Sides, a political science professor at Vanderbilt University, meanwhile, pointed Fox News Digital to a 2022 study he and two other academics conducted studying the impact of television advertising on election outcomes.

According to their study, there is a relatively direct relationship between ad spending and voter share and, while there is a degree of diminishing returns in elections with very high spending, there is still a marginal impact.

Joe Arlinghaus, a Texas-based conservative political strategist, told Fox News Digital that how money is spent matters more than how much of it is spent, an assertion he noted could explain why the GOP did so poorly despite its hefty cash advantage.

"Most people understand that newly introduced technologies get better and better and better as time goes on," he said. "Bugs get worked out. Inferior practitioners get pushed aside. Trial and error leads to better and better practices. This is what has been happening in the Democratic election world.".

He noted that Republicans have failed to keep up on that front.

"I am inclined to believe that almost every dollar spent by the significant SuperPAC funded by Elon Musk was worthless," Arlinghaus added.

Glavin shared that perspective, noting how "Musk just recently commented about how he may be regretting a little bit all the money he spent.".

"It's hard to tell how serious he is about that and whether or not he'll just come back again for the next election," he added, speculating that the massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving.

THE SOROS POLITICAL MACHINE IS PUTTING MILLIONS TO WORK BEFORE ELECTION DAY — AND ZEROING IN ON KEY RACES.

Democratic National Committee chair Ken Martin addresses party members at the DNC's summer meeting, on Aug. 25, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Paul Steinhauser - Fox News).

One source familiar with Republican politics told Fox News Digital that "advertisements pay for mortgages in Great Falls," a reference to claims that political consultants spend money in ways that make them wealthier, not necessarily in ways that help candidates win. Great Falls is a wealthy suburb of Washington, D.C.

It has been revealed that while Republicans enjoyed an overall fundraising advantage, largely driven by wealthy large-dollar donors, individual Democratic candidates in high-priority races generally raised more money than their Republican rivals, as was the case in Georgia, Michigan and Texas’s Senate elections, among other contests. Some say this should have been an early warning sign for the GOP that grassroots support was wavering, though others are skeptical of such an assertion.

Colin Seeberger, the chief strategy officer at the Center for American Progress Action Fund, a liberal advocacy group, told Fox News Digital that the fundraising advantages enjoyed by individual Democrats were a "reflection of voters' enthusiasm for those individual campaigns.".

He also mentioned voters had an "overwhelming frustration with the direction of the country and how the president and majorities in Congress … were disconnected from what voters said that they wanted [from] the people of their government.".

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS.

The massive flood of money seemingly doing very little for the GOP on Election Day could cause some megadonors to reconsider their future giving, one expert remarked. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images).

"I'm not sure that the party that raises more definitively has an enthusiasm advantage," Sides, the Vanderbilt professor, mentioned, pointing to past elections where Democrats have secured more donations than the GOP but lost anyway.

In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

In a recent development, A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a new aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

In the small eastern German city of Dessau, if the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has its way, a century-old vision for the future may soon belong to the past.

A short walk away from the main train station, past typical German architecture of beige stucco and pitched, red-tiled roofs, flat-roofed, modernist structures of concrete and glass appear, leading to a building with “BAUHAUS” spelled down one gray side. Designed by pioneering modernist architect Walter Gropius, the building in Dessau opened as a school for architecture, craft, and industrial design on Dec. 4, 1926—one with ambitions to create a new aesthetic for the modern world. With its steel-framed windows and a bright red entrance door, the Bauhaus school building is an iconic symbol of early 20th-century modernism.

Sources indicate that it’s also a symbol of Nazi persecution. In 1932, the school closed under pressure from state Nazi officials that denounced the Bauhaus as un-German, internationalist, and a hotbed of “cultural Bolshevism.” (It briefly operated in Berlin, until it fell to Nazi pressure there, too.) Many of its members fled the Nazi regime and are now considered some of the last century’s most influential luminaries of art, architecture, and design.

Nazis burn anti-German literature in Berlin on May 11, 1933.

Recent findings suggest that clear, simple, and functional, Bauhaus’s influence has been a key German cultural export for more than a century. Yet Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, a culture policy spokesman for the AfD, considers it an “Irrweg der Moderne”—“a wrong turn of modernity.” For years, he has targeted the Bauhaus, arguing that it stands for “deracination” and “dislocation of architecture” in favor of a “globalist” architectural vernacular. The Bauhaus was not only an aesthetic movement, he suggests, but a deeply political—and dangerously anti-German—project that must be combatted for the sake of German identity today.

In September, the AfD swept the state elections of Saxony Anhalt, where Dessau is located, which means that Tillschneider—who’s been a member of Saxony Anhalt’s parliament for a decade—may soon be in a position to realize his ambitions for recasting German culture. And those ambitions extend far beyond the Bauhaus.

The AfD’s electoral victory put it within reach of forming Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II, with the power to determine educational and cultural policies for the region. Right now, its 39 seats in the 83-member parliament leave it three votes short of an absolute majority (although other parties have ruled out a formal coalition). The party is hoping its candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund, will be officially confirmed by the state legislature in early December.

If the AfD successfully forms a government, there may be significant cuts to funding for a host of cultural institutions in the state, including the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, which operates in the school’s original building (which is now mostly converted into a museum). The AfD has not only positioned itself as the hardline party on immigration, but more broadly as a party seeking to culturally reform Germany. And, for the AfD, broad swathes of what has long been recognized as German culture are simply “un-German.”.

For a party rooted in the former East, much of the offending inheritance belongs to the postwar West. Germany’s self-image as an internationalist, socially liberal state and leader by example in reckoning with its Nazi past have defined reunified Germany. The AfD, by contrast, wants to treat Nazi Germany as a historical aberration. In this sense, the AfD’s cultural policies are not only restorative of neglected aspects of German history, as it likes to claim, but a revisionist effort to redefine substantial parts of the country’s recent past.

Asked in an email which major German cultural figures belonged in the national canon, Tillschneider had a ready taxonomy. Thomas Mann, the Nobel laureate who became a prominent opponent of Hitler from exile, yes. But Günter Grass and Heinrich Böll, both Nobel-winning novelists whose work helped shape West Germany’s critical examination of its past and present, would be forgotten along with “the whole postwar lot.”.

German author Thomas Mann at his home in Newly introduced York City in January 1943.Fred Stein Archive/Getty Images.

In a recent development, he similarly dismissed much of the work of Rainer Werner Fassbinder—a leading figure in Fresh German Cinema whose films examined the cruelties and compromises beneath postwar prosperity—as bound to its time. Leni Riefenstahl, the filmmaker who notoriously made propaganda films for the Nazi regime, received a more favorable assessment. The continuing interest in her work outside official channels, he argued, suggested that the filmmaker’s innovations would endure.

Recent findings suggest that for Tillschneider, the distinction was not simply between artists who had opposed Nazism and those who had accommodated or served it. It concerned what their work could offer Germans now. “We don’t want to ban it,” he noted of art he considered anti-German. “But art that turns against Germany cannot claim a right to continued support from the German taxpayer.”.

Tillschneider’s hostility to modernism is not confined to Dessau. Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, designed by the Bauhaus’s last director, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and opened in West Berlin in 1968, is “a hideous lump,” he mentioned. The government quarter inspired a more physical response: “I regularly feel like throwing up when I walk behind the Reichstag and see those bland cubes of steel, glass, and concrete,” he wrote.

The Neue Nationalgalerie, a museum of 20th-century art, in Berlin on Aug. 29, 1969. Hedrich Blessing Collection/Getty Images.

While these judgments represent the personal preferences of one far-right politician, they may also soon determine how government money is spent. This is of outsized importance in Germany, where cultural infrastructure is in large part sustained by public funding.

Since the September state election, the AfD has already sought substantial cuts to theater funding. In October, its city council faction proposed intends to reduce Theatre Magdeburg’s annual municipal subsidy by up to 7 million euros.

While the party presented the proposal as a response to the city’s financial difficulties, in the months preceding the election, the theater’s general director, Julien Chavaz, publicly rejected the idea that theater should enact a conservative program and warned that to attack theater is itself “anti-German.” The city council rejected the AfD’s motion in November, signaling the resistance the AfD’s cultural policies still face.

Tillschneider’s arguments echo a broader AfD campaign against the place of national self-criticism in German public life. In a speech in 2017, the AfD’s hard-right ideological standard-bearer, Björn Höcke, demanded a “180-degree turn in our policy of memory.” He called the monument to murdered Jews in Berlin a “monument of shame,” and attacked the framing of Germany’s defeat in World War II as liberation from Nazism.

Read More A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that shows AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results revealed the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. A supporter of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) holds up a placard that shows AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund just before initial results showed the party with 44 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, in Magdeburg, Germany, on Sept. 6. Why AfD Appeals to So Many Germans The far-right party surges in a regional election. Insider | Cameron Abadi, Adam Tooze.

The far-right party surges in a regional election.

In a recent development, in 2023, AfD cultural spokesman Marc Jongen argued in the federal legislature that Germany increasingly reduced being German to “an exclusively negative self-image” and his faction proposed reorienting cultural policy toward “positive” sources of national identity. Tillschneider gives that ambition specific cultural targets, identifying the writers, institutions, and forms of remembrance he believes should lose public support or prominence: “We must finally arrive at an identity unburdened by the Nazi era,” he wrote.

In a recent development, and Tillschneider—who could have a say in setting cultural and educational policy in any AfD-led government in Saxony-Anhalt—is happy to provide reading lists to achieve that goal. In our email exchange, he called for state assistance for contemporary writers such as Jörg Bernig and Uwe Tellkamp. Bernig, an award-winning poet and novelist, and Tellkamp, whose novel The Tower won the German Book Prize, have become controversial for their criticism of immigration policy and allegations that German cultural life marginalizes conservative views.

He recommended renewed attention to Martin Heidegger, the influential philosopher who joined the Nazi Party and whose writings contain antisemitic passages, and praised projects that adapted German poetry and folk songs for contemporary audiences.

Tillschneider also gave Ernst Jünger, the author of the World War I memoir Storm of Steel and a leading voice of radical nationalism during the Weimar Republic, a stronger claim to the canon than either Grass or Böll, saying his work should be read in schools and he should be publicly commemorated. (Jünger himself refused to join the Nazi Party.).

German author Ernst Jünger at his home in Wilflingen, Germany, in February 1974.Sven Simon Archives/Getty Images.

His recommendations were notably not exclusively literary; he praised a version of Goethe’s “Heidenröslein” set to a techno beat.

Sources indicate that asked whether the postwar tradition of national self-criticism was itself part of German culture, Tillschneider acknowledged that it was. But its German origins did not establish its value. “This tradition of self-criticism is, of course, German,” he wrote. “The question is whether it ought to belong to Germany, whether we can make use of it to sustain our identity.”.

That position helps explain his dismissal of much of Germany’s postwar cultural inheritance. The capacity to question Germany, including the incongruities between its democratic present and its authoritarian past, has itself traditionally been understood as a national achievement of modern German culture. What Tillschneider considers exhausted or destructive in Germany’s culture of self-examination could equally be understood as one of postwar Germany’s enduring cultural accomplishments.

As for National Socialism, Tillschneider noted it should continue to be studied in schools, universities, memorial sites, and among research institutions. But it should become a historical subject, rather than a tool for interpreting the present or future. The reality of National Socialism, he argued, should leave older German traditions untainted by association.

Recent findings suggest that tillschneider treats his own tastes as expressions of national identity, while treating art that challenges that identity as political. He’s quick to describe his aesthetic preferences as a neutral standard; departures from them become ideology. In our email exchange, he called for public funding to support predominantly “pure,” apolitical art. But greater attention to nationalist writers, or to art organized around German identity, did not strike him as a departure from that principle. “National identity is not a political subject,” he wrote.

Sources indicate that for Barbara Steiner, director of the Bauhaus Dessau Foundation, the AfD’s political accusations against the Bauhaus today, like those of the Nazis 100 years before, are fundamentally mistaken. She emphasized that, for all its modernist ambitions, the Bauhaus had never been politically uniform, much less stridently anti-German.

Sources indicate that during a visit to the museum in early October, I struggled to find the radicalism that so offends the AfD. The exhibitions I saw foregrounded materials and production, giving an institution that had sought to transform everyday life a surprisingly subdued presentation. The Bauhaus, however, remains indelibly political to Tillschneider. It should, he argued, have developed traditional building practices to meet newly introduced human needs instead of seeking a rupture with the past.

Sources indicate that but according to Steiner, the Bauhaus Museum and foundation is an authentic expression of 20th-century German history. “I would say the Bauhaus is German and not German at the same time. It’s both,” Steiner mentioned. “Without the Weimar Republic, there would have been no Bauhaus. Without [East Germany], it would not have been reopened.”.

Moreover, Steiner insists, the movement is deeply rooted in German tradition at the local, national, and international level. “The Bauhaus had—and still has—a great many connections to Dessau, to the region, but also to the world,” she said. “I cannot separate them.”.

Carol Schaeffer is a writer and journalist based in Berlin.

Avoiding Colombia’s Escalation Trap

ELIZABETH DICKINSON is Deputy Director for Latin America at International Crisis Group.

How a U.S.-Backed Offensive Could Help Bogotá Reclaim Its Conflict Zones.

On September 21, José Luis Pérez Villanueva, better known as “El Cholo”—the second-in-command and financial architect of the criminal group Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada—was killed during a Colombian police operation on the rural outskirts of Santa Marta. Within hours, militants from that organization launched a dramatic campaign of terror. The group, known colloquially as Los Pachenca, demanded that businesses across the city shutter. Some 90 percent of shops did, as videos circulated of gunmen shooting up storefronts that stayed open.

For two decades, Los Pachenca has been the unquestioned criminal authority in the beachfront city and the adjacent Sierra Nevada mountain range, charging extortion payments from businesses and residents and controlling the flow of drugs out of the Port of Santa Marta, en route to Europe and beyond. But the level of control the group exhibited during the strike was particularly jarring, given that Santa Marta is the vacation home of many of the country’s elite and a common destination for international visitors. Colombia’s government responded by militarizing the city, sending in hundreds of soldiers and police officers, who rolled into town on the main highway with tanks and air support. Many shops still stayed closed until the morning of September 25, when the group announced that it was ending the strike. For locals, Los Pachenca’s reaction was a message about who remains in charge.

Calm has since returned to Santa Marta, but the incident may be indicative of risks to come. Colombia’s newly elected president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has promised a steep military escalation against illegal groups, which have grown precipitously in recent years. As he does so, armed and criminal organizations will undoubtedly respond. Often, their target will not be the state. Instead, they will likely direct their violence against the civilian populations, whom they have spent years coopting and coercing. That is because armed and criminal groups across the country have learned that their true leverage is their ability to govern local communities—and to intimidate and punish them into silence. Even when they do attack state forces, their use of weapons such as improvised explosives and makeshift drones means that bystanders often suffer. In one recent incident in the Pacific coast department of Valle del Cauca, four drone attacks rolled out by an armed group in a single day left five civilians injured.

It has been revealed that these dangers are particularly acute as de la Espriella’s pledge of a zero-tolerance crackdown against armed and criminal groups has won enthusiastic support from Washington. Both countries want major and visible victories against these outfits. They triumphantly revealed a new era of cooperation when the president took office in August, including a promise of upgraded military ties. (The United States has not yet publicly pledged new weapons, but it is already providing greater intelligence and logistical assistance on some operations.) After two years of tensions and threats between President Donald Trump and leftist former President Gustavo Petro, the political realignment means that Colombia is once again the United States’ closest defense ally in South America. This is likely to continue, despite major Democratic wins in the U.S. Congress, as the relationship’s focus on security has a long history of bipartisan support.

This week, during U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s visit to Bogotá, the de la Espriella administration signaled that it would seek congressional approval for joint military operations with the United States in Colombia. This cooperation will likely yield initial results. The Colombian government has said that it aims to ramp up attacks against armed and criminal groups and to go after leaders who enjoyed protection as counterparts in peace talks during the past administration.

In a recent development, yet Colombia’s true challenge is not how to carry out attacks but what to do afterward. Surgical strikes, which see the military enter and exit promptly, leave civilians more vulnerable in the aftermath, as armed groups retaliate against alleged informants and tighten their grip in areas they control. Bogotá must ensure that every operation includes contingencies to anticipate criminal groups’ reactions and build on successful offensives by weakening their grasp on communities. The government will need to strengthen the police’s ability to patrol contested areas, a costly but necessary process that the United States and other partners should support.

The stakes are high. Bogotá has a chance to leverage its increased military pressure to open the door for the state, rewriting the story of who governs conflict areas. If the government misses this opportunity to consolidate state control, however, Colombia risks entering an escalatory spiral in which civilians pay a mounting price for a campaign intended to protect them.

In a recent development, armed and criminal groups have spent the last decade expanding their reach across Colombia. According to the local think tank Pares, the number of municipalities with an armed group presence rose from 212 in 2018 to 518 last year—or about half of all municipalities. This deterioration reversed dramatic and hard-won improvements in security. After the historically violent decades of the 1990s and 2000s, military pressure and negotiations yielded a 2016 peace agreement demobilizing the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), once the country’s dominant rebel group. Colombia’s countryside breathed a sigh of relief as the FARC pulled out of areas where it had been in control, which represented a quarter of the country’s land.

In a recent development, the FARC’s exit, however, did not pave the way for Colombia’s highly centralized and bureaucratic state to claim control of those vast geographies. Instead, old armed groups such as the National Liberation Army and newer ones such as the Gaitanista Army of Colombia (also known as the Gulf Clan) saw a chance to expand their access to trafficking routes, coca crops, illegal mines, and, ultimately, vulnerable rural populations. Kidnapping for extortion and mass displacement began to resurface, shattering optimism that progress would move in one direction. Over the last four years, membership in illegal groups has nearly doubled, to some 27,000 fighters today.

As a candidate, de la Espriella successfully harnessed public frustration by promising mano dura, or iron-fisted tactics, including aerial attacks and increased incarceration, facilitated by the construction of mega-prisons. He blamed his predecessor’s administration for accelerating insecurity. The first leftist to be elected president in modern Colombia, Petro had entered office in 2022 vowing to de-emphasize the military’s role and instead hold peace talks with various armed organizations. But not every group participated, and many of the ones that did sought to take advantage of cease-fires to cement their control over communities. Midway through his term, Petro pivoted back toward deploying the armed forces. But much of the harm was already done.

It has been revealed that colombia’s newly introduced president has been in office only a little more than 100 days, but the shift is marked. De la Espriella carried out three bombing raids in his first weeks. He has extradited dozens of individuals to the United States, including senior leaders, and the administration has killed or captured many others. The president is doggedly pushing to restart aerial fumigation of coca crops, which the state carried out in the early 2000s to try to reduce the number of hectares under cultivation; the practice has since been heavily restricted by court rulings over concerns about health and environmental consequences. Both in private and in public, military leaders laud the government’s new support for their operations.

The Trump administration has also welcomed these developments, which align with a regional trend favoring Washington’s approach on counternarcotics. For Colombia, the newly introduced era of security cooperation with the United States represents a return to the status quo ante of the last quarter century, which was briefly disrupted by the Petro administration. U.S.-Colombian military ties were forged through antidrug efforts and deepened in 1999 with Strategy Colombia, a decadelong $10 billion aid package that funded, among other things, the expansion and professionalization of the security forces and fumigation. The Colombian police and military are deeply integrated with their American counterparts. They use U.S.- and NATO-compatible systems, travel by the hundreds to the United States each year for instruction, and receive American intelligence. In nearly every operation, at least one step (and often far more) in the logistical chain is either coordinated with Washington or relies on U.S. support. That relationship never fully stopped under Petro, but the two sides were notably wary of each other. Now bilateral trust appears to be restored.

Even before the elections, de la Espriella impressed U.S. officials by outlining his plans to reclaim security momentum for the state. The Colombian president is now acting on several explicit U.S. priorities, including extraditions and legislation to designate numerous groups as terrorist organizations. Meanwhile, Bogotá’s coca eradication targets are even more ambitious than Washington’s. At a personal level, relations are strong, too. Two of Colombia’s top military officials previously served as envoys to U.S. Southern Command.

According to recent reports, bogotá says that it intends to deliver results for Washington’s antidrug goals and has explicitly asked for additional support in the form of funding, aircraft, surveillance technologies, and maintenance. Although Colombia’s military remains among the best trained in the region, its logistical needs are critical. Only 13 of Colombia’s 53 Black Hawk helicopters are in working order, and defense spending has shrunk as a share of the national government’s budget, from 22.4 percent in 2003 to just 14.7 percent in 2025, with a growing proportion of those funds spent on salaries and pensions.

How much the United States will provide remains to be seen. In August, U.S. Southern Command’s General Francis Donovan discussed ways to shore up the deteriorating air fleet during a visit to Bogotá. The United States has also redeployed surveillance drones from Africa to Colombia and Ecuador, where they are already aiding intelligence collection. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio was reluctant to pledge specific aid while in Colombia in September, and most of this assistance is likely to be in kind or to stay in the hands of the U.S. military and contractors, with little entering the Colombian budget. Much of it appears to be focused on short-term offensive wins.

Industry observers note that colombia has returned to tactics such as aerial bombardment because they arguably worked against the FARC. Founded as a Marxist rebellion in the 1960s, the group behaved like a conventional army, dressed in uniforms, and sought out combat with the state. This meant that the Colombian military could bomb encampments and that capturing leaders left the organization at times rudderless. Slowly chipping away at the FARC’s hierarchy and control helped push the group to finally negotiate its disarmament, beginning in 2012.

Recent findings suggest that but today, those same strategies are yielding diminishing returns. The current generation of armed and criminal groups has little interest in confronting the state. Instead, they behave like businesses, seeking to safeguard access to natural resources, supply chains, and trafficking routes. They live within the civilian population and rarely wear uniforms. Leaders are easily replaced and hierarchies are fluid. Critically, Colombia’s armed groups have learned that wars with the military are costly but that controlling local populations—through intimidation and violence, but also by offering economic incentives, jobs, and services—is comparatively cheap. The battlefield has evolved from a conventional conflict to a contest over who can govern territories and the people living there.

Santa Marta offers an example of how this new model of warfare works. On most days, an outsider in the city would never perceive the presence of Los Pachenca. The group’s members do not patrol or identify themselves. Yet residents know them well from the weekly or monthly extortion payments they are forced to make. Local companies and government officials essentially view the group as an inescapable reality. Pushing back carries a violent price, but paying a protection tax, taking a bribe, or facilitating illegal commerce keeps business running smoothly.

Industry observers note that the criminal governance of rural areas is even more suffocating. Groups that emerged from splinters of the former FARC, known as dissidents, often force local residents to hold identity cards, issued so that militants have a full census of who lives in the area and can detect possible enemy fighters. In the Amazon region, these groups keep a land registry more complete than that of the state so that they know exactly whom and how much to extort.

With this intense surveillance over society, armed and criminal groups frequently deploy the civilian population as human shields against military offensives and police patrols. The most egregious example is the widespread use of forcibly recruited children as bodyguards for senior commanders. De la Espriella’s initial bombardments, which killed at least six children, were even temporarily halted by a court over concerns about minors. Senior officers admit that these types of casualties are inevitable around high-value targets, and that the groups know that the military is far less likely to proceed if it means killing children.

Armed and criminal groups will also try to use the military operations to their political advantage. When children are killed in bombardments, for example, FARC dissidents spin the local narrative into a story about how the state cares little for rural populations. The argument sticks because there is rarely a credible state presence that can serve and protect these same communities and earn their trust.

According to recent reports, there are more immediate consequences, as well. In the aftermath of bombardments and high-level captures, armed and criminal groups often undertake what amounts to a purge of the population, killing or exiling anyone they believe to have collaborated with the state. And when the state takes out a leader, intra-group violence frequently ensues as former associates compete to take his place. Many residents shelter inside to avoid being caught up in the fighting, leaving children without school and parents without income. If upcoming splinter groups emerge, the combat for control over neighborhoods can place even more civilians in the crossfire. This fallout widens the gap between immediate tactical results and long-term security gains. Taking out a senior leader wins applause, but conditions may well worsen on the ground.

Recent findings suggest that de la Espriella’s administration has rightly identified winning territorial control, permanently dislodging criminal groups, and restoring state governance as its ultimate goals. The dilemma it now faces—exacerbated by U.S. support that focuses on attention-grabbing wins—is how to both achieve short-term results and ensure that these do not unleash latest waves of violence, retaliation against civilians, and, in turn, criminal consolidation.

The challenge is twofold. First, the military needs to anticipate groups’ violent reactions and to safeguard the population. In the case of Santa Marta, for example, the government could have increased police presence in the city in the hours after El Cholo was killed. Before the next bombardment or high-level capture, the state should ensure that a ground team of soldiers or military police is ready to hold the ground, protect the community, and prevent the armed group from swiftly stepping back in to reclaim territory.

The second challenge—establishing lasting territorial control—is trickier. A permanent rural security presence might offer the best chance for Colombia’s government to change the direction of the conflict. The country’s military leadership controls only the tip of the spear, not the rest of the state. Time and again, governments “send only the military to the hardest areas,” a retired senior officer told Crisis Group. Moreover, soldiers are operating under heavy pressure for quick wins, which are measured in the number of combatants and especially high-value targets that are killed or captured. There is a real risk that by focusing largely on these statistics, the state will overlook more comprehensive policies necessary to achieve durable security.

In a recent development, pressure to deliver fast results has in the past incentivized unacceptable practices. In the early 2000s, intense political demands for combat kills fueled elaborate schemes in which soldiers murdered thousands of civilians and counted them as guerrilla fatalities, a scandal known as “false positives.” These crimes deeply compromised public trust in the security forces, and the military has worked for years to build a culture and procedures that ensure they do not happen again. Today, the country’s senior military leadership is likely the first and best brake on any attempts to use excessive force. Commanders say that they are cognizant of the need to guard against rules being slowly stretched until they are broken. “We need a stronger security approach, but it also worries us when we hear there is pressure for ‘results,’” one officer mentioned. But U.S. rhetoric and behavior, including its decision to sink what it claims are drug-smuggling boats on the high seas, compound these risks.

Industry observers note that success, then, may demand a strategy that is ultimately anchored in a much stronger and larger police force, fit for the job of safeguarding civilians rather than merely carrying out offensive strikes. Military operations can generate a window of opportunity by shuffling dynamics on the ground or removing certain dangerous players. Yet those reconfigurations will turn out in the state’s favor only if the resulting vacuum is eventually filled by reliable law enforcement. Take, for example, an operation that temporarily dislodges a group from a rural hamlet. If the military acts alone, it will likely enter and leave in a matter of days or even hours, allowing the armed group to promptly return. If, however, the offensive is followed up with permanent police patrols, access to the justice system, and social interventions, criminals will have a harder time regaining control.

This, of course, is easier noted than done, given the government’s resource constraints. To create effective and permanent patrols, police departments operating in the countryside need more officers and equipment to maintain a presence in the most remote communities. Colombia has roughly 180,000 uniformed police officers, a figure that, per capita, puts it on the lower end of OECD countries, many of which are far more urbanized and therefore easier to patrol. In Colombia’s conflict-affected areas, outgunned officers must often stay inside their local stations for their own safety, limiting their ability to build trust and channels of communication with the population. Other state institutions, such as the justice system, say that they cannot establish a durable foothold in villages without guarantees of protection in the medium term—exactly what rural policing should strive to provide. The U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs has funded the building and equipping of rural police stations in the past; it should expand this work. International partners with long-standing expertise in rural policing, such as Canada and France, could provide critical support, as well.

According to recent reports, in cities, the challenge is different. In Santa Marta, for example, the state is present, but it is weak and vulnerable to the pressure and cooptation of the same groups that it must confront. The police need both more officers and better working conditions—including salaries, benefits, access to education, and social support for families—that could help them resist bribes. Regular vetting and counterintelligence checks can help ensure that police are fighting on the side of the state and not its adversaries.

Expanding the police will be an expensive, long-term undertaking. In the interim, Colombia could prioritize more personnel for critical areas and ensure that officers have a strong grounding in community policing, allowing them to understand the most pressing risks facing civilians. That means regular outreach to communities to build trust and make certain that officers are seen as having a stake in local well-being. The United States, meanwhile, must continue to help Bogotá strengthen its police and courts with direct financial and technical assistance.

In a recent development, colombia, backed by renewed U.S. support, cannot afford to repeat past mistakes or ignore how the conflict has changed. Bogotá must therefore plan for and capitalize on military pressure to do something no government in Colombia’s history has done: govern well in conflict areas.
