📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, JOSHUA A. SCHWARTZ is Assistant Professor of International Relations and Emerging Technology at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.

How Fighting Weakens Washington’s Reputation—and Backing Down May Strengthen It.

It has been revealed that in mid-February, after the United States failed to get Iran to renounce its nuclear ambitions, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an ultimatum. The Iranian leadership had to make “a meaningful deal” with Washington. “Otherwise,” he noted, “bad things happen.” Barely eight days later, the United States and Israel began the war against Iran that continues today.

That war has been criticized on many grounds, but analysts have often overlooked the basic assumption about U.S. credibility that it has tested. There is a long-held understanding that the United States’ willingness to use force to stand up for its interests is essential to deterring future adversaries—and convincing them to give in to the kind of sweeping demands the Trump administration made of Tehran. As Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, said in the early stages of the conflict, “I think both our friends and potential foes are seeing the prowess of the joint force and that also contributes to deterrence.”.

Recent findings suggest that going back to the early years of the Cold War, the concept of credibility—a state’s perceived capabilities and its willingness to use them even at high cost—has played a central role in the decisions that led to and sustained many of the United States’ largest military campaigns. The need to bolster U.S. credibility was a key force driving Washington’s strategy in Korea and Vietnam in the mid-twentieth century, and it played an key role in Iraq and Afghanistan during the so-called war on terror. American strategists today continue to assess foreign policy decisions based on how they might strengthen or weaken the country’s reputation.

But as the results of the Iran campaign have shown, a decision to use force does not always strengthen deterrence. After nearly ten months of war, and the expenditure of billions of dollars of munitions, the United States appears little closer to achieving its objectives of definitively ending Iran’s nuclear threat and ability to project power across the region, let alone securing regime change in Tehran. Meanwhile, the war has badly depleted U.S. military resources that could be used elsewhere and has further eroded the American public’s willingness to support military interventions. Rather than sending a strong signal of U.S. resolve, the Iran war risks conveying the opposite message. Vice President JD Vance argued that the reason the Republicans lost the midterm elections was the Iran war, and government officials in Tehran have gloated that “Americans remarked no to war.”.

In fact, the conventional wisdom that standing firm in a military conflict enhances a state’s credibility misses something important. As the U.S. wars in Vietnam and Iraq showed, a prolonged military campaign may leave the country more cautious about using force, and less willing to bear the costs, in the years that follow. Adversaries notice this. Given that prior efforts by the Trump administration to compromise with Tehran were criticized as “appeasement” by figures like former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence, Trump may be tempted to continue or even expand the Iran campaign. But by taxing U.S. capabilities and deepening war-weariness among the American public, escalation in Iran could instead lead Beijing and Moscow to question Washington’s appetite for future interventions.

Policymakers should be far more skeptical about using military force for the sake of demonstrating U.S. resolve, and they should be less averse to backing down. The Cold War competition with the Soviet Union convinced the United States to intervene in costly proxy wars that consumed enormous human and military resources for questionable gain, and now the strategic competition with China and Russia may do the same. These kinds of conflicts are precisely the ones that are likely to harm, rather than help, U.S. credibility. Instead of obsessing about its reputation for resolve, which it cannot control, Washington must refocus its attention on maintaining the military strength and capabilities it needs to deter its major adversaries. Sometimes the best way to preserve both the capability and the willingness to act in the future is to walk away from conflict in the present.

According to recent reports, for decades, policymakers and scholars have treated a country’s credibility as the dark matter of international politics—a hard-to-measure attribute that is nonetheless enormously notable for maintaining deterrence. In the 1960s, nuclear deterrence theorist and Nobel Prize winner Thomas Schelling went so far as to say that acquiring a reputation for resolve is “one of the few things worth fighting over.” In keeping with this, it has long been assumed that whereas standing firm communicates to adversaries and allies alike that a country is willing to run risks and bear costs to uphold its interests, backing down or seeking to compromise conveys the opposite. As a result, many U.S. leaders and strategists have drawn on the logic of credibility to justify the most hawkish policies toward adversaries: making maximalist demands, using force, and remaining in wars long past the point where their costs exceeded their benefits.

Sources indicate that vietnam was a case in point. When debating whether to send the first group of U.S. troops to Vietnam in 1965, U.S. Secretary of State Dean Rusk told President Lyndon Johnson, “If the Communist world finds out we will not pursue our commitments to the end, I don’t know where they will stay their hand.” Later, as the United States became bogged down in the war, Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton went further, arguing in a formerly top-secret memo that the primary reason for continuing the Vietnam War was to maintain America’s “reputation as a guarantor” and “avoid a humiliating U.S. defeat.” According to this logic, 58,000 U.S. soldiers and likely over a million Vietnamese people were killed not because the outcome of the war was itself crucial to U.S. interests, but because Washington worried how others—especially the Soviets—would perceive it if it withdrew.

Since the Cold War, the same justifications have been used to push the country into, and to sustain, many other conflicts. This was especially true during the so-called Forever Wars the United States was drawn into after the 9/11 attacks. On the night of 9/11, U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld stated, “We need to bomb something else [other than the relatively weak Taliban] to prove that we’re, you know, major and strong and not going to be pushed around by these kinds of attacks.” The logic of credibility not only played a role in Washington launching the Iraq war in 2003 but also locked it into the conflict, even as the costs rose and the raison d’être for the war—weapons of mass destruction—turned out to be false. As President George W. Bush said in 2006, “If we were to leave before the mission is complete, it would hurt U.S. credibility.”.

Sources indicate that conversely, strategists have been quick to criticize U.S. leaders who backed down. During the Syrian civil war, many were concerned about the reputational damage to the United States when President Barack Obama declined to respond to the Syrian government’s use of sarin gas to attack a rebel-held suburb of Damascus, thereby violating a red line that Obama had previously declared. In 2021, many foreign policy hawks reprimanded President Joe Biden for withdrawing from Afghanistan and for waiving some U.S. sanctions on Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline project. At the time, Michael McCaul, the top Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, noted, “U.S. credibility from Kyiv to Taipei cannot withstand another blow of this nature.” More recently, Trump himself has been accused of backing down against China on tariffs, which some have decried as another example of “Trump always chickens out,” or “TACO.” In each of these cases, critics argued that Washington’s failure to act has compromised the perception that the United States is willing to run risks and bear costs to achieve its objectives.

Despite the persistent assumption that U.S. credibility requires using force and refusing to back down, that thinking has been repeatedly challenged over the past decade. For one thing, experience has shown that a country’s past behavior may be a poor indicator of its present-day resolve. In April, for example, The Upcoming York Times reported that Trump believed that Iran was unlikely to attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz based on its past actions—such as its failure to mount a robust response to the U.S. and Israeli bombing of its nuclear facilities in the 12-day war in 2025. In reality, however, Iran has been far less restrained than expected in the current conflict and moved quickly not only to close the strait but also to attack U.S. allies and U.S. military bases across the region. In other words, Tehran’s failure to stand firm in 2025 had little bearing on its resolve in the present war.

It has been revealed that in any case, it is far from clear that a country’s reputation for resolve is something that it can control by its actions alone. As Keren Yarhi-Milo has explained in Foreign Affairs, “credibility is in the eye of the beholder.” Even if a state acts decisively to signal strength, an adversary may not interpret that action as reason to reconsider its behavior. For example, despite Washington’s intention to communicate high resolve by bearing tremendous costs in the Vietnam War, the North Vietnamese Communist Party Central Committee concluded in 1965 that “the domestic situation in the United States, however, will not allow them to fully utilize their economic and military power in their war of aggression.” In other words, Hanoi ignored the intended signal from Washington and refused to back down.

Other pitfalls are associated with demonstrating resolve by standing firm and fighting. At the extreme, a state that leans too much on military strength can gain a reputation for aggression in ways that undermine long-term deterrence. Napoleonic France and Nazi Germany both had strong reputations for resolve, but their offensive actions ultimately provoked other countries rather than deterring them. There is certainly a risk that U.S. actions under the second Trump administration—such as decapitating the Iranian government and threatening to annex Canada, Gaza, and Greenland—could similarly backfire. For example, there is growing evidence that U.S. allies and partners in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia are rethinking their reliance on the United States and are seeking other sources of security. Far from conceding to Trump’s demands, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described a “rupture” in relations between Washington and Ottawa and advocated for middle powers to band together to protect their sovereignty.

According to recent reports, even if using force bolsters a country’s reputation for resolve, it may harm the country’s broader credibility. For instance, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and its willingness to absorb hundreds of thousands of casualties since then has sent a strong signal about its resolve. Yet its dramatic underperformance on the battlefield against a far smaller and less well-equipped army has likely diminished the international perception of its military effectiveness. The war in Iran could similarly tarnish the United States’ military reputation. Since February, Washington has depleted at least half of its precision-strike missiles and advanced air defense interceptor missiles. It will likely take years to replenish these stockpiles given slow manufacturing times for so-called exquisite platforms. In the meantime, the United States has fewer advanced systems to draw on if China makes a move against Taiwan or if Russia attacks Poland or Estonia. For both Russia’s and the United States’ military campaigns, then, the net effect has been to reduce rather than enhance the countries’ reputation for military capability in the eyes of their respective adversaries.

Quite apart from the negative consequences that often come with decisions to use force, there is an even more fundamental problem with conventional thinking about credibility. In practice, backing down can actually be more helpful to a country’s reputation for resolve than fighting. This becomes especially clear in looking at the long-term effects of engaging in military interventions. Although the United States was victorious in World War I, the conflict produced a lingering war-weariness among the U.S. public and key policymakers. In the years after the Armistice, Americans expressed strong support for the idea that the United States should stay out of any future European war, a sentiment that was ultimately codified in the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s. Only after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, more than two years after war began in Europe, did the United States enter World War II. Fighting in World War I sent a signal of strong resolve to adversaries, but Americans’ war-weariness and resurgent isolationism in the years that followed conveyed that the United States would be less resolved to fight.

It has been revealed that this dynamic has been even more apparent in the aftermath of major U.S. wars since then. Following the Vietnam War, President Jimmy Carter declared that “young Americans should never again be sent to die in battle unless our own nation is endangered.” Consider how this kind of thinking affected adversaries’ view of the United States: In deciding to invade Kuwait in 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein assumed that the United States was intensely casualty averse and might not intervene or would back down rapidly. General Wafiq al-Samarrai, Iraq’s head of military intelligence during the Gulf War, mentioned in a 1996 interview that Saddam “thought that America’s involvement in Vietnam had badly damaged its willingness to use military power.” Although the Vietnam War was primarily fought to buttress the United States’ reputation for resolve, it had the opposite effect in practice.

In a recent development, and again, during and after the U.S. war in Iraq, Americans became skeptical of costly military interventions. As a result, recent administrations have been especially hesitant to commit ground troops in combat operations. Iran is undoubtedly aware of this so-called Iraq syndrome, which may embolden Tehran to act more aggressively without having to fear a large-scale American ground operation.

There is also experimental evidence that backing down may strengthen a country’s long-term reputation for resolve. In a survey I conducted in 2021 with 100 British parliamentarians, respondents were randomly divided into two groups. The first group read about a situation in which a hypothetical country backed down from a prior conflict. The second group read about a hypothetical country that stood firm in a prior conflict but displayed the same signs of war-weariness or “syndromes” that emerged in the United States after the Vietnam and Iraq wars. Both groups were then asked to estimate the likelihood that the country in question would stand firm or back down in a current dispute with the United Kingdom. On average, parliamentarians believed that the country that backed down in the prior dispute would have greater resolve in the current dispute. In other words, if fighting leads to war-weariness, then backing down can actually be better for a state’s future credibility.

As the U.S. campaign in Iran has demonstrated, choosing to fight to maintain a reputation for resolve is an incredibly risky gamble and may backfire. To avoid repeating the same mistake, U.S. policymakers and strategists need to rethink the relationship between credibility and fighting. First, the United States should avoid fighting altogether when the primary objective is shoring up reputation rather than defending a core national concern. If a conflict directly involves key security and economic interests, as did the U.S. Revolutionary War and World War II, then fighting can be a logical choice, assuming the United States has sufficient military capabilities to win the war at reasonable cost. But if the primary argument for the war relates to future credibility, as in Vietnam, then policymakers should be wary.

Second, if Washington determines that an adversary must be confronted with military force, then it must focus on limited, achievable objectives. Wars that drag on because they have much larger aims, or are prolonged simply for reputational reasons, may erode the country’s credibility by draining munitions and making Americans more reluctant to fight in the future. The two U.S. interventions against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq illustrate this point well. In the limited 1991 Gulf War, the United States quickly expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait at low cost and before war-weariness could set in among the U.S. public. But the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, in which Washington pursued the far more expansive goal of regime change, continued for years at high cost and made many U.S. policymakers and ordinary citizens alike less supportive of using force in the future.

Finally, policymakers should focus less on the U.S. reputation for resolve, which they cannot control, and more on the country’s military capabilities, which they can. To deter Beijing and Moscow, Washington needs to convince both adversaries that it has the ability to prosecute a modern great-power war. The problem is that, although the United States continues to have the most advanced military capabilities and weapons systems in the world, they are limited in quantity, extremely expensive, and take a long time to replace. In the course of just a few months of fighting against Iran, the United States depleted huge percentages of its advanced and expensive stockpiles of offensive and defensive missiles.

This alarming shortfall raises upcoming questions about whether the United States could sustain a longer war of attrition of the type Russia and Ukraine are fighting. Washington urgently needs to replenish its stockpiles and rethink its dependence on a small number of exquisite systems. It also needs to avoid costly conflicts that distract it from the principal threats it faces from China and Russia. Rather than making U.S. credibility stronger in the eyes of the world, continuing the war in Iran could well undermine it, just as fighting in Vietnam and Iraq did.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at new proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.

World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at fresh proposed U.S. tariffs on China and other trade partners, tensions between Ukraine and Libya over a drone attack, and the end of a long deportation battle in the United States.

World Brief will be off Thursday and Friday for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. We will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed a fresh batch of tariffs on more than a dozen major trading partners, including China, Japan, South Korea, and the European Union.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed tariff rates, which could be implemented early next year, range from 15 percent for the EU, Taiwan, and South Korea, 18 percent for most others, and rates of as much as 25 percent on India or 35 percent on Vietnam. China faces a fresh tariff rate of 20 percent, which will be stacked on top of duties still lingering from U.S. President Donald Trump’s first term—and that’s only if the trade truce between Beijing and Washington holds. (It expires in January.).

The latest tariffs are the culmination of an investigation launched this spring into alleged excess industrial capacity among nearly all U.S. trading partners. U.S. trade officials allege that other countries artificially prop up their manufacturing sectors with subsidies, promotions, tax breaks, and other measures that distort trade and disadvantage U.S. exports. U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has taken equity stakes in dozens of private companies and is actively promoting state involvement in the manufacture of everything from chips to ships.

In a recent development, china’s Foreign Ministry said the new tariffs are based on a “false proposition,” though China is one of the few countries among the 14 economies targeted that demonstrates genuine excess capacity that is harming the U.S. and global economies. Even trade specialists who are skeptical of the Trump administration’s affinity for tariffs believe that higher duties on Chinese exports are warranted.

The European Commission also hit back at the tariffs, arguing that Europe is a victim of overcapacity, not a source of the problem.

Sources indicate that the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act to levy the fresh duties—the same law that it used earlier this year to slap tariffs on 60 economies on the grounds that they do not adequately police forced labor in their supply chains. (Those tariffs were challenged in court.) The proposed new tariffs would essentially replace (and slightly raise) the rates levied earlier, implying that the question of forced labor has been solved in just a few months.

It has been revealed that the measures proposed on Wednesday are just the latest attempt by the Trump administration to find a formula to recreate in the aggregate the sweeping global tariffs that the U.S. Supreme Court struck down earlier this year. The administration has used at least four different trade authorities dating back almost a century to continue raising barriers to trade, despite polls showing that the widespread unpopularity of tariffs contributed to the Republicans’ historic midterm election wipeout.

Industry observers note that toxic explosives. The U.S. Army on Wednesday blew up nearly five tons of toxic lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The intentional detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide, a sensitive chemical compound used by the military in explosives, was originally scheduled to take place last Friday. The controlled explosion was delayed, however, amid public pushback and legal challenges from environmental groups.

Sources indicate that destroying the bomb-making material, which had been stored in the Iowa plant since 2009, was deemed necessary by the military after inspectors in March discovered that it had partially crystallized—increasing the risk of a spontaneous explosion. But the proposal to detonate the material raised concerns over the potential for toxic lead dust to spread over a large area, and many locals also mentioned they weren’t given enough notice to prepare.

Residents within five miles of the blast were urged to evacuate ahead of the detonation, while others in the vicinity were told to remain indoors.

After the detonation, the Environmental Protection Agency wrote on X that its real-time air monitors were reporting “ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region.” Adam Telle, the Army’s acting secretary, also wrote on X that the “controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success” and remarked the threat of an “uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated.”.

Ukraine and Libya. Kyiv has seemingly angered the primary military force in eastern Libya, the Libyan National Army (LNA), after attacking a Russian warship that was refueling at the Benghazi Naval Base on Sunday. Two Libyan naval officers died from wounds sustained in the Ukrainian sea drone attack. The LNA has vowed to retaliate “at the appropriate time and place, and by the appropriate means.”.

Ukraine offered no immediate public response on Wednesday, though officials remarked the previous day that Ukrainian forces hadn’t targeted Libyans in the operation.

Recent findings suggest that the incident is yet another example of how the Russia-Ukraine war has spread to other parts of the globe. Russian missiles crashed in Poland last week, and there have been repeated Russian drone incursions on NATO’s eastern flank. Ukraine also carried out a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend.

A ‘free man.’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday as part of a negotiated agreement between the Salvadoran immigrant’s attorneys and the U.S. government after a prolonged, highly publicized deportation battle with the Trump administration. “I’m happy, and I’m celebrating my freedom,” Abrego Garcia told reporters in Spanish after he landed.

In a recent development, amid the administration’s controversial crackdown on immigration, Abrego Garcia was arrested last year by federal agents in Maryland, wrongfully deported, and placed in a notorious prison in El Salvador before he was ultimately brought back to the United States. The Trump administration continued to target Abrego Garcia for deportation and aimed to send him to Liberia, but that was blocked by the courts.

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, an attorney for Abrego Garcia, said that his client left the United States a “free man” and signaled that Abrego Garcia would attempt to return once Trump is no longer in office. “Kilmar Abrego Garcia is going to outlast Donald Trump, and he’ll be back in the United States as a lawful permanent resident,” he said.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first Pakistani national to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station. Ali, who will return to Earth in a few days, told reporters that he carries “the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis.” We officially feel like underachievers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation. Owners and operators must also keep track of power purchase agreements (PPAs), warranties, service contracts, billing, compliance requirements and project-level profitability.

Sources indicate that enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a new addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform. The company announced the launch Nov. 10.

It has been revealed that the AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows. Through no-code tools, users can create AI dashboards and reports using natural-language instructions, while still establishing their own workflows, routines, data-access permissions and approval requirements.

The approach here reflects a broader shift toward renewable energy software, it’s moving beyond monitoring individual assets toward managing the financial and operational performance of entire portfolios.

Recent findings suggest that according to enSights, its EBM platform brings together energy management systems (EMS), production data, billing, PPA information, operations and maintenance, contractual obligations and compliance on a unified data foundation. That integration is central to the manufacturer’s AI strategy.

Rather than limiting AI applications to identifying equipment issues or answering generation-related questions, the platform is designed to connect energy production with the contracts and financial obligations associated with each project.

The AI Studio includes an orchestrator that coordinates specialized AI agents focused on areas like monitoring, operations, revenue, warranties, permits, lenders, insurers, and asset management. For portfolio managers, those capabilities could help reduce the time spent reviewing disconnected systems and manually reconciling information across departments. Automated reviews of contractual obligations, revenue performance and operational alerts could also help teams identify concerns earlier and direct attention to matters that still require human intervention.

The enSights AI Studio dashboard provides solar and energy storage operators with AI-powered tools for asset management, operational workflows, and financial oversight. Credit: enSights.

It has been revealed that enSights emphasized that people remain in control of the AI Team. Consumers determine which workflows the agents handle and where approvals are required. Physical asset controls remain governed by established EMS and site-level systems.

According to recent reports, the AI Studio also builds on an expanded financial management offering within the EBM platform. Its Financial Asset Management Module includes revenue assurance, contract, and obligation management, and profit-and-loss reporting.

The module is intended to provide project-level financial visibility, helping companies identify and prevent revenue losses while generating reports for investors.

The platform also includes real-time EMS, weather and tariff forecasting, along with dispatch planning intended to optimize revenue while maintaining grid safety and local compliance.

enSights claims its platform is deployed globally across more than 100,000 sites, representing over 5 GW of assets. The organization intends to demonstrate the AI Studio and its broader EBM platform at RE+ 2026.

As AI gains traction across the clean energy industry, the next competitive advantage could come from connecting operational intelligence with the financial and contractual decisions that determine how successfully renewable energy portfolios perform.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.

Attorney General Todd Blanche is mobilizing civil litigators across the Justice Department in an all-hands-on-deck push to fight tens of thousands of legal filings by detained migrants asking federal courts to review whether their imprisonment is lawful.

Blanche issued a three-page memo Tuesday calling on attorneys working outside of immigration complications to assist in the lawsuits described by Blanche as "frivolous" and an attempt to "thwart President Trump's promise to the American people to prioritize their safety and security.".

Industry observers note that the pre-Thanksgiving memo comes as the Justice Department has been hit with 97, 000 habeas corpus petition filings since January 2025, including close to 10,000 upcoming petitions filed since October. Typically, the Justice Department faces only a few hundred habeas corpus cases a year.

As President Donald Trump has made mass deportations a centerpiece of his second administration, with Department of Homeland Security figures showing nearly 1.2 million illegal immigrants removed to date, the Justice Department has seen a wave of petitions.

DHS TOUTS HIGHEST ICE DEPORTATIONS IN HISTORY, AS MULLIN NOTES AGENCY HAS BEEN ‘UNLEASHED’.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detain dozens of immigrants inside the Federal Plaza courthouse in Fresh York City on June 26 after their court appearances, amid a surge in federal court challenges from detained migrants. (Lokman Vural Elibol/Anadolu via Getty Images).

The surge in lawsuits comes after the Trump administration changed its detention policy to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the U.S. — even those who have lived in the country for years. Without access to bond hearings before immigration judges, detainees have turned directly to federal district courts to challenge their confinement.

In a post on X sharing the memo, Blanche accused judges who have granted detained immigrants' habeas corpus petitions of being "corrupt" and seeking to "release criminal aliens back into communities and avoid deportation.".

"Many of the Department's U.S. Attorneys' Offices have been overwhelmed by the influx of petitions and impracticable procedures set by the courts," Blanche wrote. "That is why it is imperative that all Department attorneys who litigate civil matters support prosecutors who have shouldered the burden of habeas petitions for nearly two years.".

SUPREME COURT TO SCRUTINIZE KEY PILLAR OF TRUMP DEPORTATION MACHINE IN BLOCKBUSTER CASE.

Sources indicate that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche testifies during a Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation hearing for his nomination to be attorney general at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, DC, on July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images).

Blanche's memo calls on attorneys from four civil litigation divisions — Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources — as well as the U.S. Trustees Program and senior leadership offices, including those of the attorney general, deputy attorney general and associate attorney general, to assist. Within the next 30 days, leadership from the respective divisions must submit an "aggressive appellate strategy" for tackling the habeas corpus claims and deploy attorneys to high-volume districts. The memo does not explicitly state how many of the department's roughly 2,000 civil litigators will be utilized.

Blanche acknowledged that divisions are already carrying "a significant workload in light of personnel reduction.".

TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN COULD STRENGTHEN ADMIN'S HAND IN LOOMING SUPREME COURT FIGHT.

A corridor inside the immigration court at the Jacob K. Javits Federal Building in Latest York on May 20, as the Justice Department mobilizes civil litigators to fight tens of thousands of habeas corpus petitions from detained migrants. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

"I also know that many attorneys have already volunteered or offered support in litigating habeas matters," Blanche wrote. "By ensuring that attorneys are assigned no more habeas matters than each attorney can adequately and zealously defend, combined with providing jurisdiction-specific resources, I hope to mitigate any significant disruption to attorneys' current dockets.".

Blanche's memo drew criticism from immigration attorneys, including Reza Mazaheri, who called the attorney general's characterization of judges as "corrupt" "slander.".

"If I walk into a courtroom and accuse a judge I disagree with of corruption, I would undoubtedly face disciplinary action," Mazaheri wrote on X. "In the public service sphere, the word 'corruption' has a distinct meaning.".

Meanwhile, Bridget Pranzatelli, a staff attorney at the National Immigration Project, told Newsweek that the influx of habeas corpus petitions is the result of a change in how the Trump administration interprets bond hearing statutes.

"Many of them would have gotten a bond hearing before this administration suddenly changed its interpretation of a decades-old law to fill beds that private prison companies get paid for," Pranzatelli said in a statement.

#202737. Breaking: The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2553 w)

Breaking: The Only Way to End the Netanyahu Era

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026.
  • Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.
  • As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AYMAN ODEH served in the Knesset from 2015 to 2026. He is the former leader of the Joint List and the Hadash party.

Arab Citizens of Israel Can Bring Change, but They Can’t Do It Alone.

As the Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot struggles to assemble a governing coalition following last month’s elections, Israel finds itself in a familiar political predicament. The parties opposed to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition command a clear majority in the Knesset, with 67 of its 120 seats. Yet the four Jewish-led parties in Eisenkot’s camp hold just 48 seats, leaving them unable to form a government on their own. The impasse echoes the prolonged political deadlock between 2019 and 2021, when Netanyahu’s supporters and his opponents remained locked in competing parliamentary blocs, and four consecutive elections failed to produce a stable governing majority.

But one thing is different this time. Israel’s Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Raam, are stronger than ever. Powered by extraordinary turnout among Arab citizens of Israel, they won a record 19 seats in the Knesset: 11 for the Joint List and eight for Raam. This political mobilization is important in itself, demonstrating Arab voters’ overwhelming desire for change and their recognition of the importance of participating in elections. But its significance goes far beyond the number of seats they have won. Together, the Arab parties now have the potential to be a decisive force in an anti-Netanyahu coalition, providing the parliamentary backing needed to form a government. The proof of this power has already been shown: on November 17, Arab support was crucial in the vote to replace the Likud speaker of the Knesset with a speaker from Eisenkot’s party. Now they have a historic opportunity to put the country on a different path.

As the first and former leader of the Joint List, I know how much is at stake. In 2019, I helped lead a groundbreaking effort to give Arab-led parties a direct voice in the Israeli political system. We took an enormous political risk by endorsing Benny Gantz, then a former chief of staff of the Israeli military and Netanyahu’s principal rival, as a candidate to form a government. We did so despite our profound political and ideological differences with him. Although that effort ultimately fell short, with Gantz choosing to pursue a “unity government” with Netanyahu instead, it established an crucial precedent: by showing a willingness to work with Jewish political forces with whom they had deep disagreements, parties representing the Arab public had a real chance to prevent a Netanyahu-led far-right government from holding power.

It has been revealed that today, after nearly four years of disastrous leadership by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, that possibility has become far more urgent. It will take political courage on both sides. Eisenkot must be able to offer something to the Arab-led parties, and the Arab-led parties will need to be comfortable offering support to a government that they may not agree with on many problems. But the remarkable Arab turnout and the sizable Israeli majority that is now against Netanyahu have pointed to a way forward. Not only Israel’s future but also its place in the region and the world may depend on the willingness of its leaders to engage with the country’s Palestinian minority. Ultimately, such a partnership will be essential to building the trust between Jews and Arabs that is a prerequisite to achieving any real progress toward a viable Israeli-Palestinian peace. This is the real choice now facing Israel: whether Israelis are prepared to replace the politics of supremacy and exclusion with a politics of equality.

Recent findings suggest that the factors that drove record numbers of Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in October have been years in the making. Although the country’s Arab citizens make up more than 20 percent of the Israeli electorate and have long made vital contributions to Israeli society as doctors, lawyers, engineers, high-tech professionals, and in many other fields, the Israeli right has for decades demonized them as enemies: a fifth column and a threat to the state. In recent years, this hostility has increasingly manifested itself in harassment and open racism at universities and workplaces, in the media, in the parliament, and in everyday life.

According to recent reports, yet it would be a mistake to assume that Arab exclusion has been driven only by Netanyahu and the radical right. Zionist parties of the center and the left have also contributed, by keeping a distance from Arab voters or simply ignoring them. The belief that Jewish citizens should ultimately determine the country’s political direction while Arab citizens must remain within whatever limits have been set for them runs deep in Israeli politics. Netanyahu understood early on how to turn this contradiction into a political strategy. Since the 1990s, he has repeatedly used the same formula: inciting his supporters against Arab citizens, delegitimizing Arab representatives in parliament, and convincing Jewish Israelis that a government that relies on Arab political support would somehow be illegitimate.

Industry observers note that these tactics proved to be among Netanyahu’s most effective political tools, especially given that Arab-led parties have long been some of his biggest foes. He didn’t need to convince everyone to support his Likud party or its various coalition partners. He only needed to convince enough people, including Jewish Israelis who opposed him, that working with Arab-led parties was dangerous and unacceptable. Netanyahu’s strategy also helped suppress Arab turnout. Since the Arab-led parties had little chance of changing the status quo, Arab voters had little incentive to vote: for many years, a significantly lower proportion of Arab citizens went to the polls than did their Jewish counterparts.

That began to change in 2015 with the creation of the Joint List, which for the first time brought together four parties representing the Arab public on a single electoral ticket and which became the third-largest faction in the Knesset. By embracing a broader vision for our society, grounded in Jewish-Arab solidarity and opposition to the racism of the right, the Joint List demonstrated that Palestinian citizens of Israel could play a new and more influential role in the country’s political system. Then, under my leadership in 2019, the Joint List decided to back Gantz’s bid to unseat Netanyahu. The decision was highly controversial, both within the Arab electorate and across Israeli society. Many Arab voters were deeply ambivalent about supporting a potential government led by a former army chief whose political positions, particularly on the status of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the occupation, differed sharply from their own. Nevertheless, we were prepared to take that political risk because we understood that defeating Netanyahu was more notable.

In a recent development, in practice, our willingness to cooperate with the Zionist opposition was not, in fact, reciprocated. The Jewish opposition parties wanted our votes but could not bring themselves to accept us as equal political partners. And, ultimately, Gantz decided to form a government with Netanyahu instead. Nevertheless, the experience showed that Jewish-Arab political cooperation could open up new horizons for a large segment of the public. Since then, every time that Arab-led parties have recommended or supported the effort of a Jewish candidate to form a government, or whenever the Israeli center-left has depended on their support, additional segments of Israeli society have become more open to this kind of cooperation.

It has been revealed that in 2021–22, an Arab party, Raam, joined the short-lived government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. I had serious reservations about the model of partnership that emerged, which seemed to rest on the expectation that Arab political representatives would limit their involvement to civilian and domestic matters, while refraining from addressing political and national questions, particularly the occupation and the Palestinian glitch. I reject this distinction. We are part of the Palestinian people, and our identity and political concerns cannot be separated from our citizenship in Israel.

In a recent development, but these kinds of slow and painful steps are how political change often happens in national struggles. It does not always begin with a moral or democratic awakening. Sometimes, it begins with pragmatic necessity. When there is no other option, people begin to reconsider what had once been seen as impossible. In the current election, that dynamic has become even more important. After the unending crisis of the past four years, many Israeli voters, including both Arabs and Jews as well as the leaders of most of the Zionist opposition parties, have concluded that getting rid of the Netanyahu government is more necessary than ever.

It has been revealed that in recent past elections, voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel has generally remained between 50 and 60 percent. What explains the unprecedented 20-percentage-point surge in turnout in the October election? Three developments stand out: the war of annihilation in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of Palestinians; the daily racism and hostility that Arab citizens now face in the streets, in public spaces, and in virtually every aspect of their lives; and the crime that has spiraled out of control in Arab communities under the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose policies have allowed it to flourish, and the relentless settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank enabled by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. All the grief and frustration accumulated over these years were brought to the ballot box.

But there was another crucial factor as well. In the run-up to the election, Arab citizens, following the nearly even polls between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, could see in black and white just how much the outcome would depend on them. Voting this time would be more than a political choice. It was for many a personal responsibility and a way of taking control of their own future. That is why hundreds of thousands of Palestinian citizens of Israel made their way to the polls, defying years of efforts to silence them and undermine their political agency. Many understood that the future direction of the country might be quite literally in their hands.

In a recent development, I saw elderly people, like my friend Jumah from Jisr al-Zarqa, taking to the streets and campaigning for the Joint List. Many of them had lived through the 1948 nakba, or “catastrophe,” which accompanied Israel’s establishment and involved terrible massacres, the destruction of hundreds of Palestinian villages and towns, and the displacement of around 750,000 Palestinians. I saw young people debating politics in the cafés and restaurants of my beloved Haifa, persuading their friends to vote. I saw women and men from Nazareth, Umm al-Fahm, Sakhnin, Rahat, Akko, Kafr Yasif, Majd al-Krum, and countless other towns and villages united by a shared sense of purpose. I saw political consciousness become a living, collective force. For a moment, the boundaries between generations and communities seemed to disappear.

Sources indicate that the result marks a remarkable advance of the process of Arab participation in the Israeli political system that began in 2019. In this election, Arab citizens of Israel turned out in record numbers, dramatically narrowing the historical turnout gap with Jewish voters. And that has made another political reality increasingly clear: Israel’s liberal and centrist camp cannot form a government without the parties that represent the Arab public. If it excludes them, as well as the ultra-Orthodox and the far right, it will not reach the 61 seats needed. This is the demographic reality. Israeli Jews who oppose Netanyahu must decide whom they are willing to build a political future with.

According to recent reports, the debate about what Eisenkot should do and whether he should ask for Arab support is now unfolding beyond the Knesset, in people’s homes, in cafés, in universities, and on the street. It is a deeply controversial question, and many Israelis disagree strenuously about it. Yet for the Arab-led parties, gaining sufficient importance to be able to provoke these conversations is an achievement. The fact that this debate is even taking place reveals how the political process has caused Israelis to consider possibilities that until recently seemed unimaginable.

Recent findings suggest that in the end, Eisenkot may have few other options if he wants to replace Netanyahu, as he has promised. In most cases, political parties support coalitions to advance positive changes and achieve concrete goals. But there are moments when political cooperation is necessary for a different reason: to prevent something far worse. The most immediate and overriding objective today is to bring an end to the far-right Netanyahu government. That is a priority on which both the Zionist opposition and the Arab-led parties can agree.

Recent findings suggest that beyond this shared basic goal, the Arab-led parties should use their political influence to work on two levels. First, they must seek tangible improvements in their constituents’ lives: combating organized crime in Arab communities, securing budgets, addressing the housing crisis, ending the brutal treatment of Palestinians living under occupation in the West Bank, and pushing for a permanent cease-fire and the reconstruction of Gaza. These are fundamental concerns of human dignity and civilian life. On a broader level, they should continue to push for real progress on Israeli-Palestinian peace that is ultimately based on two states coexisting, side by side.

Industry observers note that I do not expect the current Israeli political establishment to embrace these positions, but that does not mean that the Arab parties should not raise them at every opportunity. At the same time, the Arab parties can use their newfound political clout to build alliances between Jews and Arabs around shared political and strategic goals. The resulting partnerships must be about more than parliamentary arrangements; it must also create the foundations for a different future. That will require Jewish and Arab citizens of Israel to engage with one another on the basis of equality, rather than mere political convenience.

It has been revealed that thus far, Eisenkot has given few indications that he is prepared to go down this path. Since the election, it has been encouraging to see him condemn Netanyahu for fueling what he described as a “racist and violent” campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens. Yet many of the mainstream Zionist parties in Eisenkot’s camp have vowed not to work with the Arab parties. Still, Eisenkot must consider what that would mean. Thirty years from now, people will ask how Jewish supremacy became so normalized that even politicians who called themselves democrats accepted the exclusion of one-fifth of their fellow citizens. They will ask why Israel’s opposition could recognize the danger posed by Netanyahu’s government but not confront the assumptions that made his politics possible.

Industry observers note that there is an irony in the fact that, in a country that seeks to keep political hegemony exclusively in Jewish hands, the Palestinian minority, after decades of struggle for political recognition and equal rights, has emerged as one of the most significant forces shaping the country’s political future. We have come to understand that we must be courageous and cooperate with the Zionist parties of the center and left in order to oust Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich. The question now is: Do these parties, which call themselves democratic and liberal, have the same courage?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Ukraine attacks Russian vessels in Libya in “response to Russia’s war,” Gambia wins a landmark case at the International Court of Justice, and African nations respond to a disappointing United Nations climate summit.

According to recent reports, kyiv claimed responsibility on Monday for a recent attack on two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, including the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships. The vessels had been docked at the Benghazi naval base when the attack occurred on Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has described the operation as “exemplary” and noted that it was in “response to Russia’s war.”.

Yet security experts warn that conducting drone strikes within a region that is not involved in the Russia-Ukraine war could set a dangerous precedent, especially as they fear Africa is becoming a proxy theater in the conflict.

The United Nations mission in Libya, known as UNSMIL, has called for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation” into the drone strikes. “Libya cannot afford, and must not become, a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.

Industry observers note that kyiv has confirmed that seven Ukrainian-made naval drones had been launched from a “mothership” in the region, though it did not clarify how they were transported there. Some unverified Libyan sources have alleged that Tripoli’s U.N.-recognized government may have aided Ukraine, which Tripoli strongly denied.

Both of Libya’s rival administrations—the government in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah, and a Russia-backed government based in Benghazi, controlled by Gen. Khalifa Haftar—have denounced the attacks.

Following the 2024 fall of the Assad regime in Syria, where Russia operates a naval base, Moscow has sought alternative military footprints in Africa, including by pursuing airbases in eastern Libya. Syria served as a logistical hub for transferring troops and arms to landlocked Sahel nations, where Russia’s mercenary Africa Corps helps fight jihadists.

With Syria growing closer to the United States and Europe, Libya now serves as that hub, explained Ulf Laessing, the head of the Syria/Iraq program at the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung and the author of Understanding Libya Since Gaddafi.

It has been revealed that “Ukraine is trying to hit Russia wherever they can. It’s difficult for Ukraine to hit Russian targets where the Africa Corps is based in the Sahel,” Laessing said. “It’s more efficient and easier to do it where Russia is basically bringing goods.”.

Zain Hussain, a researcher at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, said that “through this attack, Ukraine is showing that it can target Russia’s geopolitical interests as well as fighting a war with Russia at home.”.

It has been revealed that the strikes come amid increasing concern that the war in Ukraine is spreading to other African countries. Ukrainian drone specialists have been deployed to Libya, Mali, and Sudan, according to a September CNN report. A source also told CNN that troops from Chad, Niger, and Burkina Faso had traveled to Mali to receive drone training from Ukrainian soldiers, though several experts told me that the evidence for this is speculative at best.

Meanwhile, in the Sahel, multiple media reports have accused Ukraine of supporting and training northern Mali’s Tuareg separatists in recent years as a means of wearing down Russian forces there.

It has been revealed that experts suspect Ukrainian drone assistance in the Tuareg ambush that killed dozens of Russian Wagner mercenaries and Malian soldiers in 2024. At the time, Andriy Yusov, a spokesperson for Ukrainian military intelligence, said that the rebels had been given the “necessary” information to carry out the attacks. Yusov’s comments prompted Mali to sever relations with Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of supporting a “barbaric” attack by terrorists.

Industry observers note that analysts also suspected Ukrainian involvement in the brief insurgent takeover of Mali’s strategic town of Kidal earlier this year by Tuareg and al Qaeda-linked jihadists. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry has officially rejected the allegations.

Ukraine’s latest attacks are unlikely to disrupt eastern Libya’s ties with Russia, Laessing remarked, especially as Moscow needs “a country on the way to the Sahel.” Still, they add a layer of complexity to long-standing violence and drone warfare in Sahelian nations, said Virginie Baudais, the director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s Sahel and West Africa program.

As Baudais put it, the “internationalization of the conflict” in the Sahel will only contribute to “the escalation of violence, with the highest cost for civilian populations.”.

Monday, Nov. 23, to Friday, Nov. 27: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention’s public health conference is held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Friday, Nov. 27: The deadline for councils in South Africa to elect their leaders.

Somalia-UAE rift. Last week, Somalia expelled the United Arab Emirates’ ambassador and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, citing ​violations of the country’s sovereignty that amounted to an “open invasion.”.

The dispute stems from growing Emirati ties with Ethiopia and the Somalian breakaway regions of Somaliland and Puntland. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud also accused the UAE of having played a role in Israel’s recognition of Somaliland last December in a statement to Somalian state news agency SONNA.

The UAE’s state-owned DP World and its subsidiaries operate ports in those breakaway regions. They have expanded the Berbera port in Somaliland and are developing a road corridor connecting it to landlocked Ethiopia. In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding to eventually recognize Somaliland’s independence in exchange for naval and commercial access to Berbera.

A Upcoming York Times report using satellite imagery recently found that the UAE has turned airports in Berbera and Bosaso, a city in Puntland, into military facilities.

In response to Somalia’s latest move, the UAE stated its embassy in Somalia had been closed since January, after Mogadishu canceled bilateral agreements, and it strongly denounced the “escalatory and hostile approach” by the Somali government amid the latest diplomatic spat.

ICJ ruling. Gambia, the smallest nation in mainland Africa, won a landmark case last week when the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar committed genocide in its 2017 military campaign that killed at least 10,000 members of the Rohingya Muslim minority community and displaced more than 700,000 into neighboring Bangladesh.

It has been revealed that A Muslim-majority nation, Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019. Now, the ruling has possible implications for South Africa’s ICJ genocide case against Israel for its operations in Gaza.

Both Myanmar and Israel have defended their actions as counterinsurgency operations. But in its decision, the court considered a pattern of mass killings, the razing of homes, and forced exodus. That finding “gives South Africa more avenues ​to argue for genocide” in Gaza, Israeli legal expert Yuval Shany told Reuters.

In a recent development, COP31’s failures. This year’s U.N. climate summit, known as COP31, in Turkey ended on Sunday without an agreement after references to phasing out fossil fuels were removed from the draft text. Despite being the most attended COP to date, some observers have called it the “worst” one ever.

In a recent development, at the summit, African delegations voiced discontent with financial commitments for climate adaptation. Wealthier nations pledged only $50 million in total to the climate adaptation fund, far short of the $300 million annual target. They also largely offered loans rather than grants. The United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, France, Italy, and Australia did not make any funding commitments.

Africa, which is home to 17 percent of the world’s population, is responsible for just 4 percent of global carbon emissions. Yet the continent faces disproportionate impacts from climate change.

It has been revealed that the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), chaired by Ghana, rejected attempts to weaken both finance targets and the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. It said that the debate on fossil fuels had “overshadowed” broken promises on adaptation finance.

Recent findings suggest that “Those who were arguing about whether we should get fossil fuels in the cover decision or not were producers, exporters, importers and users of fossil fuels,” AGN chair Antwi-Boasiako Amoah said. “It was hypocrisy.”.

AFCON verdict. Senegal was reinstated as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champion in a much-anticipated ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport on Tuesday.

Senegal initially won the final against Morocco 1-0 in extra time in January. Two months later, however, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) stripped the country of its title, awarding it to Morocco because Senegalese players temporarily walked off the pitch to protest refereeing decisions.

The court overturned CAF’s decision because the match was allowed to conclude. “By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” the court noted in a statement. Morocco plans to appeal the decision.

Sudanese excavations. Last week, archaeologists unearthed the original floor of the largest medieval church in Nubia, in northern Sudan’s ancient city of Old Dongola. It was part of Makuria, one of three Christian Nubian kingdoms that existed from the sixth to 16th centuries.

In a recent development, the church was first discovered in 2021, but excavations were suspended two years later following the outbreak of Sudan’s civil war. Operations resumed last year in the abandoned city, which has managed to escape widespread destruction from the conflict so far.

UNESCO estimated that more than 100 cultural sites have been damaged, looted, or destroyed since fighting began in Sudan in April 2023.

It has been revealed that troll farmers. In HumAngle, Shade Mary-Ann Olaoye reports on U.S.-based social media influencers exploiting false narratives of a Christian genocide in Nigeria for engagement and donations. These accounts have posted artificial intelligence-generated content and videos from elsewhere in Africa, including Somalia, as supposed evidence of persecution in Nigeria.

Industry observers note that as the creators “continue to spread misinformation, concerns are growing that their online influence could have real-world consequences,” Olaoye writes. “Campaigns like these can deepen ethno-religious fault lines, shape political decisions, and fuel reprisal attacks.”.

AI bioweapons. In Rest of World, Danai Nesta Kupemba reports on researchers at a small AI lab in Ghana who “jailbroke” their own drug-discovery AI model, which allowed them to quickly design thousands of toxic molecules, to warn about the potential for AI bioweapons misuse.

“Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists,” Kupemba writes.

JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes.

Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative.

In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics.

GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION.

"At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote.

"We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics.".

Industry observers note that illinois Gov. JB Pritzker holds a news conference in Chicago, Wednesday, June 24, 2026, to sign the Reproductive Health Records Privacy Act (HB 5295) into law. (Terrence Antonio James/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images).

Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states.

Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions.

"It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz remarked in a press release.

"Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states.".

Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids.".

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS.

In a recent development, students raising hands while teacher asking them questions in classroom. (iStock).

Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — New York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets.

Industry observers note that the U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead.".

Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name.".

"May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added.

Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state.

A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images).

"You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi remarked about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program.

"You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he mentioned in relation to his decision.".

Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment.

The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight.".

Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

Against an Axis of Anything

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W.
  • According to recent reports, those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

Reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

According to recent reports, those picking up a copy of the Economist this week might have been struck with an unpleasant sense of nostalgia. Readers were greeted with a front cover emblazoned in red and black, with a screaming headline proclaiming the “axis of malice.”.

Industry observers note that reminiscent of the war on terror and all its fearmongering excesses, this headline was widely mocked on social media as a reminder of the George W. Bush era. Those who mocked it were in turn derided as naive; growing connections among Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea surely, others argued, prove the existence of such an axis.

Sources indicate that but most of this debate missed the point. No one—or at least very few people—would deny that we have seen ties between China and Russia grow in recent years. The use of the axis framing, however, and of language like “malice,” creates a narrative that does not necessarily exist in practice. It suggests that the only response to growing alignment between these states is adversarial, inhibits us from any real debate about the extent and scope of this coordination, and perhaps most importantly, suggests that this process of alignment is inevitable, rather than something that can be molded or changed. Such overly simplistic and Manichaean visions weaken, rather than strengthen, our ability to understand the world.

None of this is upcoming. The “axis of evil” first emerged as a term in President George W. Bush’s 2002 State of the Union address, where he referred to Iran, Iraq, and North Korea as countries that endangered freedom around the world. Even at the time, the inclusion of the line in the speech was somewhat strange: It took place just a few months after the Sept. 11 attacks, and shortly after the United States had invaded Afghanistan, yet the three countries representing “evil” had nothing to do with either.

But the overblown rhetoric helped to build support for Bush’s Freedom Agenda by reinforcing the idea that dictatorships around the world could endanger daily life in democracies. It attempted to tie the war on terror to the legacy of World War II through implicit comparison to Nazi Germany and imperial Japan. The speech had real-world consequences: It helped the Bush administration build the case for its war against Iraq and undermined the thawing of relations between the United States and Iran that had started shortly after 9/11.

Recent findings suggest that since that time, there have been repeated attempts to revive the axis concept to make a political or foreign-policy point. In just the last few years alone, there have been articles about the axis of authoritarians, the axis of upheaval, and the axis of aggressors. All these formulations offer authors the same opportunity: Pick a selection of nations and define them, not on their own terms, but on yours.

Industry observers note that the axis of authoritarians, for example, relies on regime type to tie together its members, though the list of countries involved (Russia, Iran, North Korea, Belarus, and China) includes unreformed Soviet-style totalitarian regimes, kleptocratic dictatorships, and party-rule capitalism. This group includes one of the world’s richest states—and one of its poorest. The axis of upheaval, meanwhile, is defined by countries’ opposition to the United States, or by their shared commitment to “overturn[ing] the global order.” In truth, one could have an axis of almost anything; one is reminded of the old joke from around the time of Bush’s initial speech that suggested groupings including the “axis of just as evil” and the “axis of countries that aren’t the worst but certainly won’t be asked to host the Olympics.”.

Sources indicate that jokes aside, there is no denying that there are points of convergence and cooperation between the states referenced in these groupings. The reporting that accompanies the axis of malice story, for example, identifies a shared interest in the sanctions-busting “shadow” oil trade as a key area of cooperation among Russia, China, and Iran. Russia and China are cooperating on defense industrial issues, while Russia has built stronger ties with both Iran and North Korea due to its war in Ukraine and the search for cheap drones and easily replaceable domestic labor. There is a very clear case to be made that the bilateral relationships between many of these countries have grown stronger in recent years, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

Skeptics of the axis notion, however, would argue that many of these areas of cooperation were themselves driven by U.S. sanctions policy, not sought out by the states in question. There are clear tensions between Moscow and Beijing when it comes to North Korea, while China has been remarkably reticent in supporting either Russia’s war in Ukraine or Iran’s war with the United States. The evidence of growing bilateral ties between states is not matched by evidence of a common front among these states. Looked at holistically, many of their actions can just as easily by explained as states that find their interests—at least temporarily—pointing in the same direction.

According to recent reports, regardless of whether the skeptics or proponents of a more integrated partnership among these states are correct, this is an crucial debate. Indeed, it’s vitally important for U.S. policymakers to understand the scope and extent of cooperation between potentially adversarial states. The axis framing itself, however, is fundamentally unhelpful in moving these debates forward.

In a recent development, for one thing, formulations like axis of upheaval and axis of malice are less descriptive than prescriptive: They always suggest the worst, and push policymakers toward the most hawkish options. Consider the description of growing China-Russia trade ties as “collusion.” Were the U.S. to engage in such trade with any of its allies, this would be considered perfectly normal behavior. Indeed, think tank papers are published every day in Washington talking of ways to increase resilience among the U.S. and its allies. The states under discussion here are often bad actors in world affairs, but adjectives like malice or upheaval suggest Manichaean actors implacably opposed to the United States with no nuance involved.

The all-or-nothing nature of this framing also makes it more difficult to have discussions about the actual extent and scope of coordination between these states. By portraying them as a unified front—and by framing the debate as whether or not there is an axis—discussion often glosses over more interesting and potentially useful questions: Where specifically are these states cooperating? Are there limits to that cooperation? Are there issues on which they compete or where their interests diverge?

Perhaps most importantly, the notion of an axis of unfriendly states overlooks questions about how we got to this point—and whether this set of affairs must necessarily endure. At least some of the recent collaboration between these states has been shaped by U.S. policy choices, from sanctions and export controls on Russia and China, to the war in Iran and its effects in raising global oil prices. U.S. policymakers may still judge these policies to be worth the cost, yet it is fundamentally misleading to suggest that Russia, China, Iran, and others are pulling together purely to oppose the United States, when at least some of that coordination is a response to U.S. actions.

To put it another way: The idea of an axis of upheaval attempting to overturn global order strips the United States of its agency and replaces it with predestination. This is particularly important when it comes to the policy responses. An axis of aggression cannot be reasoned with and it cannot be split apart, leaving little for the United States to do other than resist it. A more nuanced understanding of why these states cooperate—and where their common cause might fail—offers opportunities for the U.S. to undermine that alignment. If we understand the causes of adversaries’ alignment, we might be able to predict or even prevent it.

It’s easy to see why the language of the axis persists: It sells. But there’s a reason why such headlines should be relentlessly mocked. They deny us the ability to have a nuanced debate and reduce our policy options to an unsatisfying binary. For those who take U.S. foreign policy seriously, it’s past time to retire the axis of evil for good.

In a recent development, emma Ashford is a columnist at Foreign Policy and senior fellow with the Stimson Center’s Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct assistant professor at Georgetown University and the author of Oil, the State, and War. X: @EmmaMAshford.
